milestones.title: A healed amputation in a Bornean cave burial
milestones.summary: The skeleton of a young person buried in Liang Tebo cave shows that part of the left lower leg was removed, probably in childhood, and that the person survived for years afterwards.
milestones.explanation:
Excavators working in the limestone karst of East Kalimantan found a burial in which the lower third of the left leg was missing. The cut through the shin bones is clean and oblique, and the bone ends show healing, which the team interpreted as a deliberate amputation rather than an accident or animal attack.

The individual appears to have survived the operation and lived for another six to nine years before being buried with care. That implies someone controlled bleeding, managed the wound and looked after a person with reduced mobility in a tropical setting where infection would have been a serious risk.

The find challenges a long-held view that complex surgery only emerged with settled farming societies around 10,000 years ago. Until this report, the oldest widely accepted amputation came from a Neolithic farmer in France, about 7,000 years ago.

date.basis: The excavation report describes the burial as at least 31,000 years old; summaries of the paper give 31,000–30,000 years ago. Converted to BCE approximately, using 1950 as the reference year for 'years ago'.

milestones.locationNote: The cave's exact position is not given in the sources consulted; the marker covers the karst region.

people.name: An unknown foraging community
people.role: Carried out the amputation and cared for the patient

people.name: Tim Maloney and an Indonesian–Australian team

milestones.whatChanged: Pushes the earliest known evidence of a successful surgical amputation back by roughly 24,000 years, and into a foraging rather than a farming society.
milestones.whyItMattered: It shows that sophisticated surgical knowledge, including how to limit blood loss and infection, could exist among Ice Age foragers in tropical Asia.
limitations: We do not know how the operation was done, what tools were used or why the limb was removed.
A single skeleton cannot show how common such operations were.
The interpretation rests on one study; no independent re-analysis was found.

sources.citation: Maloney TR, Dilkes-Hall IE, Vlok M, et al. Surgical amputation of a limb 31,000 years ago in Borneo. Nature 2022;609(7927):547–551.
sources.supports: Date (at least 31,000 years ago), location (Liang Tebo, East Kalimantan), amputation of distal third of left lower leg, survival 6–9 years, previous oldest case c. 7,000 years ago.

sources.citation: Early limb amputation in Borneo. The Past (Current World Archaeology), 15 November 2022.
sources.supports: Reported date range 31,000–30,000 years ago; clean cut through tibia and fibula; excavation in 2020.

milestones.sourceNote: All accounts derive from one excavation report (Maloney et al. 2022). The magazine report summarises that paper and is not independent confirmation.

milestones.title: Flint tools used on a decayed tooth, Villabruna
milestones.summary: A molar from a hunter-gatherer buried in the Dolomites about 14,000 years ago carries scratch marks inside a large cavity, interpreted as an attempt to clean out the decay with pointed flint.
milestones.explanation:
Researchers examined the teeth of a young man buried at Riparo Villabruna, a rock shelter in the Belluno Dolomites. A large carious cavity in a lower molar had striations that, under the scanning electron microscope, resemble cut marks made by pointed flint tools.

The marks were made while the man was alive and the authors argue they show intentional, if partial, removal of decayed tissue. They suggest early dental treatment grew out of the much older habit of toothpicking, using scraping and levering rather than drilling.

Attempts to detect residues of any medication applied to the tooth were inconclusive.

date.basis: The burial was directly radiocarbon dated to c. 14,160–13,820 calibrated years before present (BP = before 1950), i.e. roughly 12,210–11,870 BCE.

people.name: Gregorio Oxilia, Stefano Benazzi and colleagues

milestones.whatChanged: Extends evidence of deliberate work on a diseased tooth back before farming, several thousand years earlier than drilled teeth from Neolithic Mehrgarh.
milestones.whyItMattered: Suggests that people treated dental pain long before the dietary changes of agriculture made tooth decay common.
limitations: The purpose is inferred: to remove decay and/or restore the tooth's function.
Similar marks can come from cutting meat held in the teeth; the authors argue the cavity's position makes this unlikely.
No evidence of any medicine applied to the tooth was found.

sources.citation: Oxilia G, Peresani M, Romandini M, et al. Earliest evidence of dental caries manipulation in the Late Upper Palaeolithic. Scientific Reports 2015;5:12150.
sources.supports: Direct date 14,160–13,820 cal BP; Riparo Villabruna (Sovramonte, Belluno); ante-mortem striations from pointed flint tools; interpretation and limitations.

milestones.sourceNote: One peer-reviewed study. A follow-up by the same group (Riparo Fredian, 2017) reports related evidence but is not independent.

milestones.title: Early skull surgery in Europe — and a re-examined 'first'
milestones.summary: Healed openings in skulls from the Dnieper Rapids and from Ensisheim in Alsace have both been called the earliest trepanation in Europe. The Ensisheim case has since been reassessed.
milestones.explanation:
Trepanation, cutting or scraping an opening in the skull, is one of the oldest surgical procedures for which there is physical evidence. Healing around the edge of the hole shows that a person survived the procedure.

In 1997 a skull from a Neolithic cemetery at Ensisheim, dated to about 5100 BCE, was published as the earliest unequivocal trepanation. A year later, a skull from the Vasilyevka II cemetery in the Dnieper Rapids region, dated 1,000–2,000 years earlier, was reported with a fully healed opening.

In 2022 a re-examination of the Ensisheim skull argued that its two lesions may not be healed surgical openings at all and that disease cannot be excluded. The story is a reminder that a 'first' can be overturned in either direction, by new finds or by new readings of old ones.

Why people performed trepanation is unknown for these early cases. Later traditions show both therapeutic uses, such as treating skull fractures, and other motives.

date.basis: Vasilyevka II cemetery: radiocarbon determinations calibrated to 7300–6220 BCE (2σ). Ensisheim burial: c. 5100 BCE as reported in 1997.

locations.name: Ensisheim 'Les Octrois', tomb 44
locations.role: Published as healed double trepanation in 1997; diagnosis questioned in 2022

people.name: Mesolithic and Neolithic communities of eastern and central Europe

milestones.whatChanged: Established that cranial surgery with survival was practised in Europe by at least the seventh millennium BCE, while showing how fragile priority claims are.
milestones.whyItMattered: Trepanation was practised independently in many parts of the world. These cases are among the earliest well-studied examples.
limitations: A healed opening documents a procedure, not its purpose or its benefit to the patient.
Openings in the skull can also result from injury, disease or decay after burial, so diagnosis requires careful study.
Dates for Vasilyevka II are for the cemetery, not the individual skeleton.
milestones.contested: Ensisheim was described as the earliest 'unequivocal' trepanation in 1997; Lillie (1998) reported an older case; Escolà (2022) argues neither Ensisheim lesion is clearly a healed trepanation.

sources.citation: Alt KW, Jeunesse C, Buitrago-Téllez CH, et al. Evidence for stone age cranial surgery. Nature 1997;387(6631):360.
sources.supports: Original report of the Ensisheim case.

sources.citation: Lillie MC. Cranial surgery dates back to Mesolithic. Nature 1998;391(6670):854.
sources.supports: Vasilyevka II location (Dnieper Rapids, c. 400 km south-east of Kyiv), calibrated dates 7300–6220 BCE, complete closure of the aperture; Ensisheim dated to 5100 BCE.

sources.citation: Escolà M. La chirurgie crânienne du Néolithique alsacien : état de la question. Bulletin de la Société préhistorique française 2022;119(2):295–324.

sources.citation: Walker AA. Neolithic surgery. Archaeology 1997;50(5).
sources.supports: Ensisheim described as the earliest unequivocal evidence (1997); purpose unknown.

milestones.title: Drilled molars at Neolithic Mehrgarh
milestones.summary: Eleven molar crowns from nine adults buried at Mehrgarh carry neat drilled holes made in life, evidence of a local tradition of proto-dentistry lasting centuries.
milestones.explanation:
Mehrgarh, at the foot of the Bolan Pass, is one of the earliest farming villages known in South Asia. In its Neolithic graveyard, researchers identified eleven drilled molar crowns belonging to nine adults, women and men.

The holes were bored with tiny flint drill tips, probably the same tools that villagers used to perforate beads. Wear on the edges of the holes shows the teeth continued to be used for chewing, so the drilling was done on living people.

The authors argued that the holes, on back teeth where they would scarcely be visible, were unlikely to be decorative. Whether the drilling relieved pain or treated decay cannot be proven; no filling material survived.

date.basis: The graveyard is dated 9,000–7,500 years ago (roughly 7000–5500 BCE). The drilled teeth span this period, so the practice persisted rather than occurring once.

people.name: Alfredo Coppa, Luca Bondioli, Roberto Macchiarelli and colleagues

milestones.whatChanged: Provides the earliest known evidence of drilling living human teeth, as a practice repeated over many generations.
milestones.whyItMattered: Shows a craft skill (bead drilling) being turned to bodily care, and that early farming communities attempted dental intervention.
limitations: The purpose is inferred; therapeutic intent is likely but not demonstrated.
The practice does not appear in later periods at the site.

sources.citation: Coppa A, Bondioli L, Cucina A, et al. Early Neolithic tradition of dentistry. Nature 2006;440(7085):755–756.
sources.supports: Eleven drilled molar crowns from nine adults; Neolithic graveyard in Pakistan dated 7,500–9,000 years ago; a long tradition of proto-dentistry.

sources.citation: Microscopy reveals early Neolithic dentistry. Microscopy Today (Cambridge University Press), published online 14 March 2018.
sources.supports: Authors' reasoning that the drilling was not decorative because the holes would hardly be visible.

milestones.sourceNote: The evidence comes from one research team's 2006 report; the second item summarises it.

milestones.title: Covered drains in every street of Mohenjo-daro
milestones.summary: In the third millennium BCE, the Indus city of Mohenjo-daro was built with drains along every street and lane, connected to bathing floors and wastewater chutes in houses.
milestones.explanation:
Mohenjo-daro, on the right bank of the Indus, is the best-preserved city of the Indus civilisation. Its lower town was laid out on a strict plan. Street drains of fitted baked brick, sealed with mud mortar, ran along every street and lane, even in the poorest quarters, and were mostly covered with bricks or limestone blocks that could be lifted for cleaning. Larger drains had corbelled roofs high enough for workers to enter.

Inside houses, bathing floors and vertical pipes in the walls carried wastewater out to the street drains. The same drains were maintained and rebuilt over long periods. The so-called Great Bath, a large waterproofed tank, was emptied through a covered drain.

The system shows organised management of water and waste on an urban scale. What its builders understood about the link between waste and disease is unknown.

date.basis: UNESCO dates the city to the 3rd millennium BCE. The drains were built and rebuilt over a long period within this range.

people.name: Inhabitants and builders of the Indus city

milestones.whatChanged: Shows city-wide management of wastewater built into urban design.
milestones.whyItMattered: One of the earliest known examples of sanitation planned at the scale of a whole city.
limitations: We cannot tell whether health was a motive; the drains may reflect ideas of cleanliness, ritual or simple practicality.
Similar features exist at other Indus cities such as Harappa; Mohenjo-daro is the best preserved, not necessarily the first.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro (List no. 138).
sources.supports: Most ancient and best preserved urban ruin in the Indus Valley, 3rd millennium BC; strictly planned lower town.

sources.citation: UNESCO World Heritage Centre. State of conservation report, Archaeological Ruins at Moenjodaro.
sources.supports: Located on the right bank of the Indus, 28 km from Larkana; best preserved urban settlement in South Asia.

milestones.title: The Kahun papyrus on women's health
milestones.summary: A papyrus from the town of Lahun in Egypt, written around 1800 BCE, sets out diagnoses and treatments for gynaecological complaints, fertility and pregnancy. It is the oldest surviving Egyptian medical papyrus.
milestones.explanation:
The papyrus was excavated at el-Lahun, near the Faiyum, by Flinders Petrie in 1889 and is now in the Petrie Museum at University College London (UC 32057). It dates from the Twelfth Dynasty of the Middle Kingdom.

The text is divided into short sections, each describing a woman's complaint, how to recognise it and how to treat it, with remedies applied to the body or taken by mouth rather than surgery. It also covers fertility, pregnancy and contraception.

Older medical texts exist elsewhere: a Sumerian medical text from around 2000 BCE is known from Mesopotamia.

date.basis: Dated on palaeographic and archaeological grounds to the Twelfth Dynasty (Middle Kingdom), which ended c. 1773 BCE.

milestones.whatChanged: Preserves the earliest systematic written guidance on women's reproductive health from Egypt.
milestones.whyItMattered: Shows that maternal and reproductive health was a distinct field of medical knowledge nearly four thousand years ago.
limitations: Its explanations reflect Egyptian ideas of the body, such as the womb causing symptoms elsewhere; many remedies would not be effective.
Being the oldest surviving Egyptian medical papyrus says nothing about where such knowledge began.

sources.citation: Science in Ancient Egypt (Saxon Academy of Sciences, Leipzig). Kahun Gynaecological Papyrus (UC 32057), with bibliography including Collier M, Quirke S. The UCL Lahun Papyri (BAR International Series 1209, 2004), 58–64.

milestones.title: The Edwin Smith papyrus: injuries examined case by case
milestones.summary: An Egyptian papyrus copied around 1600 BCE presents 48 cases of wounds and fractures, each with examination, diagnosis, prognosis and treatment. It includes the earliest known written descriptions of the brain's surface and of spinal injury.
milestones.explanation:
The scroll is named after the American dealer Edwin Smith, who bought it near Luxor in 1862; it is now held by the New York Academy of Medicine. It was copied around 1600 BCE from an older text whose date is uncertain.

Its 48 cases are ordered from the skull down to the chest and upper arm, and each follows a fixed formula: a description of the injury, the diagnosis, a prognosis and the treatment, with explanatory notes. Several cases describe skull fractures exposing the brain and its coverings, and injuries of the neck that cause paralysis.

The main text is strikingly free of magic, though spells and recipes appear on the other side of the papyrus.

date.basis: The surviving copy is dated to about 1600 BCE. The original it was copied from is older; estimates range widely and are uncertain.

locations.name: Thebes region, where the papyrus was bought in 1862
locations.role: Acquired near Luxor; original findspot and place of writing unknown

milestones.locationNote: The papyrus was bought, not excavated, so the marker shows where it surfaced rather than where it was written.

people.name: An unknown Egyptian author and later copyist

milestones.whatChanged: Shows a structured, observation-based approach to injuries, including the judgement that some cases should not be treated.
milestones.whyItMattered: It is the oldest known surgical treatise and a key witness to Egyptian clinical reasoning.
limitations: It is a copy; the date and authorship of the original are unknown, and the 1862 purchase means its findspot is unrecorded.
Claims that it reflects a 'scientific' medicine separate from magic are partly modern framing; the same scroll contains spells.

milestones.title: Babylon's Diagnostic Handbook is edited
milestones.summary: Around the mid-eleventh century BCE the Babylonian scholar Esagil-kīn-apli produced a standard edition of Sakikkû, a long series of tablets linking symptoms to diagnoses and prognoses.
milestones.explanation:
Mesopotamian healers had been writing down medical knowledge for centuries. Esagil-kīn-apli, chief scholar to King Adad-apla-iddina, gathered and edited the diagnostic omen series known as Sakikkû, 'symptoms', creating the version that later scribes copied. His own catalogue explaining the new edition survives in Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian copies.

Each entry follows a conditional formula: if a patient shows certain signs, then the diagnosis or outcome is this. The handbook covers symptoms throughout the body and records disease names, prognosis and supposed causes, which often included divine or demonic agency alongside natural explanations.

The work shows diagnosis organised as a systematic body of knowledge long before Greek medicine.

date.basis: During the reign of Adad-apla-iddina, as named in Esagil-kīn-apli's catalogue; reign dates themselves vary slightly between chronologies.

locations.name: Babylonia
locations.role: Region where the edition was made; copies survive from Assyria and Babylonia

people.name: Esagil-kīn-apli
people.role: Chief scholar (ummânu) who edited the series

milestones.whatChanged: Created a standardised reference that tied observable signs to diagnosis and prognosis.
milestones.whyItMattered: One of the earliest large-scale systematisations of diagnosis, and a reminder that diagnostic reasoning did not begin in Greece.
limitations: The handbook mixes clinical observation with divination; its causes are often supernatural.
Esagil-kīn-apli edited an existing tradition rather than composing it from scratch.

sources.citation: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative. Medical texts (CDLI Wiki).
sources.supports: Diagnostic Handbook by Esagil-kīn-apli during the reign of Adad-apla-iddina (1067–1046 BC); symptoms, disease names, prognosis and causation; casuistic formula; earlier Middle Babylonian diagnostic texts.

milestones.title: 'On the Sacred Disease' argues epilepsy is natural
milestones.summary: A treatise in the Hippocratic collection, written around 450–400 BCE by an unknown author, insists that epilepsy is no more divine than any other disease and that its seat is the brain.
milestones.explanation:
Epilepsy was widely called the 'sacred disease' and treated with purifications and charms. The author of this short treatise attacked that view, arguing that people called the disease divine only because they did not understand it.

He described seizures from observation, loss of voice, foaming at the mouth, clenched hands and loss of awareness, and located their cause in the brain, which he regarded as the organ of thought and feeling. His mechanism, phlegm blocking passages from the brain, came from humoral theory and has not survived, but the insistence on natural causes did.

The treatise belongs to the Hippocratic Corpus, a collection of writings by many authors traditionally linked to Hippocrates of Kos. Its author is not known, and earlier thinkers such as Alcmaeon of Croton had already identified the brain as the seat of intelligence.

date.basis: Usually dated to the second half of the fifth century BCE on stylistic and historical grounds.

locations.name: Greek-speaking Aegean world
locations.role: Author and place of writing unknown; the Corpus is traditionally linked to Kos

milestones.whatChanged: Argued explicitly that a feared condition had natural, brain-based causes rather than divine ones.
milestones.whyItMattered: An early challenge to supernatural explanations of disease and to the stigma attached to epilepsy, which nonetheless persisted for centuries.
limitations: The proposed mechanism (phlegm from the brain) was wrong.
Attribution to Hippocrates himself is traditional, not established.
Natural and supernatural explanations coexisted in many traditions, including Mesopotamian and Egyptian medicine.

sources.citation: Theodore WH, in: Third International Congress on Epilepsy, Brain and Mind, part 1. Epilepsy & Behavior (PubMed Central).
sources.supports: First surviving text devoted to epilepsy, usually dated 450–400 BCE; Alcmaeon and Democritus may have written earlier.

sources.citation: The evolution of the concepts of seizures and epilepsy: what's in a name? (PubMed Central).
sources.supports: Hippocratic collection, around 400 BC, by an unknown physician; scientific view of epilepsy.

milestones.title: Two thousand years of skull surgery in the Andes
milestones.summary: More trepanned skulls are known from Peru than from the rest of the world combined. Healing on the bone shows survival improved over time, reaching high rates in the centuries before the Spanish conquest.
milestones.explanation:
Over 800 skulls with surgical openings have been recovered from burial caves and excavations in coastal and highland Peru, the earliest dating to around 400 BCE. Analysing healing around the openings, John Verano and colleagues showed that early practitioners lost about half their patients, but that techniques were refined over the centuries.

Between about 1000 and 1400 CE, survival rose to as high as 91 per cent in some samples, and in the Inca period only around 17 to 25 per cent of patients died before their skulls began to heal. Some skulls bear several openings.

The researchers note that these outcomes compare favourably with nineteenth-century cranial surgery, but there are no written records explaining how Andean practitioners avoided infection.

date.basis: From the earliest dated trepanned crania studied (c. 400 BCE) to the end of the Inca period at the Spanish conquest.

locations.name: Central Andes: coastal and highland Peru

people.name: Andean practitioners across many cultures, including the Inca
John W. Verano, Anne Titelbaum and David Kushner

milestones.whatChanged: Documents a long, evolving surgical tradition in which outcomes measurably improved.
milestones.whyItMattered: Shows independent development of cranial surgery in the Americas, and that pre-modern surgeons could achieve high survival.
limitations: Healing shows survival, not why the operation was done or whether it helped the patient's condition.
Most skulls were collected in the late 1800s and early 1900s, and their contexts are not always well recorded.

sources.citation: Kushner DS, Verano JW, Titelbaum AR. Trepanation procedures/outcomes: comparison of prehistoric Peru with other ancient, medieval, and American Civil War cranial surgery. World Neurosurgery 2018;114.
sources.supports: More prehistoric trepanned crania in Peru than anywhere; nearly 2,000 years of practice from 400 BC; survival rates analysed.

milestones.title: Medical manuscripts buried at Mawangdui
milestones.summary: A Han-dynasty tomb at Mawangdui, sealed in 168 BCE, held the earliest surviving Chinese medical manuscripts, including a formulary of more than 250 prescriptions now called Recipes for Fifty-Two Ailments.
milestones.explanation:
Tomb 3 at Mawangdui, near Changsha, probably belonged to Li Xi, a young nobleman of the Western Han. When it was excavated in 1973, a lacquer case in the coffin chamber held a library of texts written on silk, bamboo and wood. Among them were medical manuscripts that had been unknown for two thousand years.

The best known, now called Recipes for Fifty-Two Ailments, contains more than 250 prescriptions and treatments. Other manuscripts deal with the body's channels and with treatment by moxa, a plant material burned on or near the skin. Because they predate the classic medical canons, they show Chinese medicine at an earlier, less systematised stage.

The tomb gives a firm latest date; the texts themselves were composed and copied earlier, at dates that are uncertain.

date.basis: The tomb was sealed in 168 BCE, so the manuscripts were written before then. When the texts were composed is uncertain.

locations.name: Mawangdui Tomb 3, near Changsha (Kingdom of Changsha)

milestones.whatChanged: Revealed medical writing from before the classic Chinese canons, otherwise lost.
milestones.whyItMattered: Changed scholars' understanding of how Chinese medicine developed and when its classic texts were compiled.
limitations: These are the earliest surviving manuscripts, not the beginning of Chinese medical writing.
How well the remedies worked is unknown, and they reflect ideas about illness very different from today's.

sources.supports: Seven medical manuscripts on three sheets of silk from Mawangdui Tomb 3, recovered in 1973; burial dated 168 BCE; first published 1983.

milestones.title: The Compendium of Suśruta describes surgery, including rebuilding the nose
milestones.summary: The Suśrutasaṃhitā, a Sanskrit medical treatise composed in layers about two thousand years ago, is a foundation of Ayurveda and contains detailed surgical instructions, including the reconstruction of noses and ears with skin flaps.
milestones.explanation:
The Compendium of Suśruta is one of the classical texts of South Asian medicine. It covers diagnosis and therapy but is especially known for its surgical teaching, including the plastic repair of the nose and ears.

Its nasal reconstruction, using a flap of the patient's own skin, was later known in Europe as the 'Indian method'. The text was written in several authorial layers, and later commentators worked with revised versions. The oldest dated manuscript, from 878 CE and preserved in Kathmandu, records an earlier version than modern printed editions.

Popular and clinical literature often dates Suśruta to 600 BCE or even earlier. Philological research does not support these dates.

date.basis: The Suśruta Project dates the work to about two thousand years ago and stresses its many authorial layers; internal evidence suggests it is later than the Carakasaṃhitā. The earliest dated manuscript is from 878 CE. The range shown is deliberately broad.

locations.name: South Asia (place of composition unknown)
locations.role: Where the text was composed is not known

milestones.locationNote: No reliable place of composition is known, so the treatise appears in the list and timeline but not on the map. Its oldest dated manuscript is preserved in Kathmandu.

people.name: Suśruta (traditional author) and later redactors
people.role: Authors of successive layers of the text

milestones.whatChanged: Set down a systematic surgical curriculum and techniques such as flap repair of the nose.
milestones.whyItMattered: The Indian method of nasal reconstruction influenced European plastic surgery, and the text remains central to Ayurveda.
limitations: The common clinical claim that Suśruta lived around 600 BCE (or 1000–800 BCE) is not supported by textual scholarship.
The surviving text mixes layers from different periods, so not every technique can be dated to the same time.
milestones.contested: Dates for Suśruta and the Compendium vary by more than a millennium across publications; philologists date the work to about two thousand years ago.

milestones.title: Tetracycline in the bones of ancient Nubians
milestones.summary: Bones from a population that lived in Sudanese Nubia around 350–550 CE contain the antibiotic tetracycline, probably from fermented grain or beer. Whether its use was deliberate is debated.
milestones.explanation:
In 1980, examining Nubian bones under ultraviolet light, the anthropologist George Armelagos and colleagues noticed a green-yellow fluorescence typical of tetracycline, an antibiotic produced by Streptomyces soil bacteria. Sceptics argued that the signal could have come from microbes invading the bones after burial.

In 2010, the chemist Mark Nelson and colleagues dissolved samples and confirmed by mass spectrometry that tetracycline was embedded in the bone itself, including in a young child. The quantities suggested regular consumption over long periods. The team proposed that the source was grain fermented into a beer-like gruel and contaminated with Streptomyces.

The authors believe the Nubians knew what they were doing. That is an interpretation: the chemistry shows exposure, not intention or medical purpose.

date.basis: Date range of the burial population studied (the 'X-Group' period).

milestones.locationNote: The burial sites lie in Sudanese Nubia; the marker shows the region rather than a specific cemetery.

people.name: Nubian communities of the Nile valley
people.role: Produced and consumed the fermented food or drink

people.name: George Armelagos
people.role: Bioarchaeologist who first noticed the fluorescence

milestones.whatChanged: Showed that people ingested an antibiotic substance some 1,500 years before antibiotics were discovered in the laboratory.
milestones.whyItMattered: Raises the possibility that fermented foods were used, knowingly or not, in ways that affected infection, and shows how chemistry can test archaeological claims.
limitations: The evidence shows consumption, not that the substance was used as medicine or that it improved health.
The claim that Nubians deliberately produced it is the researchers' interpretation.
milestones.contested: Earlier critics attributed the fluorescence to post-burial contamination; the 2010 chemical analysis addressed that, but the question of intent remains open.

milestones.title: Al-Razi distinguishes smallpox from measles
milestones.summary: The Persian physician Abu Bakr al-Razi wrote a treatise that set out how to tell smallpox and measles apart at the bedside, based on careful clinical observation.
milestones.explanation:
Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (865–925) was born in Rayy, near present-day Tehran. He directed the hospital in his home town and, at the invitation of the caliph al-Muktafi, a large hospital in Baghdad, before returning to Rayy.

His short treatise, Kitab al-Judari wa al-Hasbah (On Smallpox and Measles), describes the warning signs of each disease, such as continuous fever, back pain and itching of the nose, and how their course differs. It reads as the work of someone who watched many patients closely, and his other writings include case records of patients he or his students treated.

The treatise was translated into Latin many times and, much later, into other European languages, shaping how physicians far from Rayy and Baghdad described these diseases.

date.basis: Written during al-Razi's working life (he died in 925). The year of composition is not known.

locations.name: Rayy
locations.modern: Shahr-e Rey, south of Tehran, Iran
locations.role: Al-Razi's birthplace; he directed its hospital

locations.name: Baghdad
locations.role: He directed a large hospital here at the invitation of the caliph al-Muktafi

milestones.locationNote: Where the treatise itself was written is not known; both cities where he practised are shown.

people.name: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (Rhazes)

milestones.whatChanged: Gave physicians a systematic, observation-based way to distinguish two common eruptive fevers.
milestones.whyItMattered: Accurate differentiation underpins prognosis, isolation and, much later, prevention. The treatise remained in use for centuries through translation.
limitations: Smallpox-like diseases were described in other traditions before al-Razi; claims that he gave the 'first' description of smallpox should be treated cautiously.
His explanations of cause followed humoral theory, not contagion by specific agents.

milestones.title: Geel's families take in people with mental illness
milestones.summary: From around the thirteenth century, pilgrims seeking cures for mental illness came to the shrine of St Dymphna in Geel, and local families began boarding them in their homes. The tradition of family foster care continues today.
milestones.explanation:
Geel, a small town in Brabant, became known through the legend of St Dymphna as a place of healing for people regarded as possessed or insane. When the church and its infirmary could not house everyone who came, townspeople took them into their own homes as boarders.

Over centuries this became a system: residents with mental illness lived with host families, joined in daily work and community life, and returned to institutional care when they needed it. In the nineteenth century, asylum reformers across Europe and North America visited and debated the 'colony of Gheel' as an alternative to confinement.

The World Health Organization's 2001 report on mental health described Geel as one of the best examples of how communities can care for people with mental illness. A family foster care programme still operates there.

date.basis: Histories place the earliest infirmary and the boarding model in the 13th century; other accounts say families took in patients 'over 600 years ago'. The exact start is not documented.

people.name: Host families of Geel
people.role: Provided care and homes over generations

people.name: Boarders with mental illness
people.role: Lived as members of host households

milestones.whatChanged: Established care for people with mental illness within ordinary family and community life rather than in confinement.
milestones.whyItMattered: Geel became an enduring reference point for community-based mental health care and for recovery-oriented approaches.
limitations: Its religious origins lay in ideas of possession and miraculous cure, not in medical theory.
Historical conditions for boarders varied, and nineteenth-century observers disagreed about whether the system was humane.

milestones.title: Ibn al-Nafis describes blood passing through the lungs
milestones.summary: In a commentary on the anatomy of Ibn Sina's Canon, written in the mid-thirteenth century, the physician Ibn al-Nafis argued that blood cannot pass through the wall between the heart's ventricles and must reach the left side through the lungs.
milestones.explanation:
Galen had taught that blood seeped from the right to the left side of the heart through invisible pores in the dividing wall, the septum. Ibn al-Nafis, a Syrian-born physician who trained in Damascus and worked in Cairo, rejected this. The septum, he wrote, has no passages; blood from the right ventricle must travel through the lungs, mix with air, and return to the left ventricle.

This is a description of the pulmonary, or 'lesser', circulation, some three centuries before the European anatomists Michael Servetus and Realdo Colombo set out similar ideas in the 1550s. His commentary was then largely forgotten in the West until an Egyptian physician, Muhyo al-Deen al-Tatawi, came across a manuscript in Berlin around 1930.

Whether European anatomists knew of his work through translation is debated; many historians consider the sixteenth-century descriptions independent. His reasoning appears to have been largely theoretical rather than based on dissection.

date.basis: Written during Ibn al-Nafis's career (he died in 1288); sources place the commentary between the late 1230s and 1260.

locations.name: Cairo (Mamluk Egypt)
locations.role: Where he practised; place of writing uncertain

people.name: Muhyo al-Deen al-Tatawi
people.role: Rediscovered the manuscript in Berlin around 1930

milestones.whatChanged: Overturned the Galenic idea of pores in the heart's septum and proposed that blood passes through the lungs.
milestones.whyItMattered: A correct account of the pulmonary circulation, centuries before it reappeared in Europe, and a case study in how knowledge can be lost and rediscovered.
limitations: He did not describe the full circulation of the blood; his account of the rest of the body remained Galenic.
His conclusions seem to rest more on reasoning than on dissection.
milestones.contested: Whether Servetus or Colombo knew Ibn al-Nafis's work is unresolved; many historians treat the European descriptions as independent.

milestones.title: Cairo's al-Mansuri hospital opens
milestones.summary: In 1284 the Mamluk sultan al-Mansur Qalawun founded a large endowed hospital in Cairo with separate wards for different conditions, including mental illness, open to patients regardless of sex, origin or religion.
milestones.explanation:
Hospitals called bimaristans, a Persian word meaning 'house of the sick', had developed across the Islamic world in earlier centuries, in cities such as Baghdad, Damascus and Córdoba. The al-Mansuri bimaristan in Cairo was among the largest and best documented.

Funded by a charitable endowment (waqf), it combined treatment, a pharmacy and teaching. Its wards were organised by type of illness, including surgery, infectious disease and mental illness, and separated by sex. Physicians bequeathed libraries to it; Ibn al-Nafis left it his house and books when he died in 1288.

The bimaristan is an example of organised, institutional health care with public funding and professional staff, long before such hospitals became common in Europe.

date.basis: Year of foundation, as given in multiple histories of Islamic hospitals.

people.name: Physicians, pharmacists and attendants of the bimaristan

milestones.whatChanged: Combined specialised wards, pharmacy, teaching and charitable funding in one institution.
milestones.whyItMattered: Bimaristans were a model of institutional care, including for mental illness, and influenced hospital design elsewhere.
limitations: Frequently repeated figures for its size (such as 8,000 beds) are not reliable.
It built on a long tradition of earlier bimaristans and was not the first.

milestones.title: Ragusa orders a period of separation for travellers
milestones.summary: In 1377, during recurring plague, the Great Council of Ragusa required people arriving from plague-affected areas to spend 30 days apart before entering the city.
milestones.explanation:
Ragusa (present-day Dubrovnik) was a self-governing trading city on the Adriatic whose prosperity depended on ships and caravans. After the Black Death, its Great Council decreed in 1377 that visitors from plague-endemic areas must stay in isolation for 30 days, the trentino, before they could enter.

The idea that waiting out a period of time would reveal whether someone was carrying disease spread to other cities in the following decades, and the period was extended to 40 days, the quarantino, from which 'quarantine' comes. Venice opened a permanent plague hospital, a lazaretto, on an island in its lagoon in 1423.

The measure worked on observation, not on any understanding of plague bacteria or fleas. It also imposed real costs on travellers and trade, a tension that has accompanied quarantine ever since.

date.basis: Date of the Great Council's decree.

milestones.whatChanged: Turned the separation of people at risk into a written, enforceable rule with a defined duration.
milestones.whyItMattered: Time-limited quarantine became a standard public-health tool, used against plague, cholera, yellow fever and, in the twenty-first century, SARS and COVID-19.
limitations: Isolation of the sick is far older; what is documented here is a formal, time-limited quarantine of arrivals.
Its effectiveness against plague in this period cannot be measured from surviving records.
milestones.harms: Quarantine and sanitary cordons were often enforced harshly and could fall hardest on the poor, on minorities and on people stigmatised as carriers of disease.

sources.citation: Tognotti E. Lessons from the history of quarantine, from plague to influenza A. Emerging Infectious Diseases 2013;19(2):254–259.
sources.supports: Quarantine first introduced in 1377 in Dubrovnik; first permanent lazaretto opened by Venice in 1423; social and ethical issues.

milestones.title: Stadaconan healers cure Cartier's crew of scurvy
milestones.summary: In the winter of 1535–36 Jacques Cartier's crew was dying of scurvy at Stadacona. Domagaya, son of the Stadaconan chief, showed them a remedy called annedda, an infusion of evergreen bark and leaves, prepared by two local women.
milestones.explanation:
Cartier's ships were frozen in near the village of Stadacona, on the site of present-day Quebec City, from November 1535. By February 1536 only 10 of his 110 men were in good health, and 25 eventually died. Cartier tried to hide his crew's weakness from the local people.

He learned of the cure from Domagaya, whom he had taken to France the year before. At Cartier's request, Domagaya had two women prepare the remedy from the bark and foliage of a conifer the Stadaconans called annedda, probably eastern white cedar. The sick recovered quickly.

The knowledge did not stay with the Europeans. When Roberval's party wintered near the same place in 1542, about 50 of 200 men died of scurvy, apparently without using the remedy.

date.basis: The remedy was given during the winter of 1535–36, after the crisis reached its peak in February 1536 (Cartier's account).

milestones.whyItMattered: An early, well-documented case of European survival depending on Indigenous medical knowledge, and of that knowledge failing to be retained.
limitations: The plant cannot be identified with certainty; eastern white cedar is the most common identification.
The account comes from the French side; Stadaconan understanding of the remedy is known only through it.
milestones.harms: Cartier had seized Domagaya and his brother Taignoagny in 1534 to train them as interpreters, and in 1536 he took their father Donnacona to France, where he died.

milestones.title: Vesalius's Fabrica rebuilds anatomy on dissection
milestones.summary: In 1543 Andreas Vesalius, professor at Padua, published De humani corporis fabrica in Basel: seven books of human anatomy based on his own dissections, with detailed woodcut illustrations that corrected many errors inherited from Galen.
milestones.explanation:
Vesalius, a young professor of anatomy and surgery at the University of Padua, insisted that reliable knowledge of the body must come from examining cadavers rather than from ancient texts. He spent much of 1542 dissecting and working with artists to prepare the woodcuts, then took the work to the printer Johannes Oporinus in Basel, where it appeared in 1543.

The Fabrica was the first profusely illustrated anatomy book. By comparing the human body with Galen's descriptions, many of them based on animal dissection, Vesalius showed where the ancient authority was wrong. It changed how anatomy was taught and set observation above textual authority.

It was not a solitary achievement: Vesalius built on a broader movement of anatomical study and on the skills of the artists and printers who made the book.

locations.name: University of Padua (Republic of Venice)
locations.role: Dissections and preparation of the book (1542)

milestones.whatChanged: Made direct dissection and accurate illustration the basis of anatomical knowledge.
milestones.whyItMattered: Founded modern anatomy and encouraged physicians to test ancient authority against observation.
limitations: The artists responsible for the woodcuts are not securely identified.
Advances in anatomy were the work of many people; the Fabrica is the best known of them, not the only one.
milestones.harms: Anatomy depended on the bodies of executed criminals, used without their consent; Vesalius assembled a skeleton in Basel from an executed man, Jakob Karrer.

milestones.title: Smallpox inoculation practised across Asia, Africa and the Ottoman world
milestones.summary: Long before vaccination, people in China, parts of Africa and the Ottoman Empire deliberately gave healthy people a mild smallpox infection to protect them. European and colonial American physicians learned the practice from these traditions.
milestones.explanation:
Inoculation, later called variolation, introduced material from a smallpox sore or scab into a healthy person. The resulting illness was usually milder than naturally caught smallpox and left lifelong immunity, although some inoculated people died and they could infect others.

The earliest written discussion of the practice is in a Chinese book first published in 1549, which describes blowing powdered scab material into the nose. A Chinese tradition dates its invention to 1567–1572; a much-repeated claim that it began around 1000 CE rests on little documentation. Claims of ancient origins in India are not supported by Sanskrit medical texts, and an eighteenth-century report of Indian practice is doubtful.

In Constantinople, physicians reported to the Royal Society in London in 1714 and 1716 that inoculation had been introduced by a Greek woman around 1660 and had spread after an epidemic in 1700. Lady Mary Wortley Montagu had her son inoculated there and in 1721 had her daughter inoculated in London. In the same year, Onesimus, an enslaved African man, described inoculation in his homeland to the Boston minister Cotton Mather. The origins of the practice remain obscure, and it may be much older than any surviving record.

milestones.title: Nahua physicians record Indigenous plant medicine
milestones.summary: In 1552, at the Colegio de Santa Cruz in Tlatelolco, the Nahua physician Martín de la Cruz composed an illustrated herbal of Indigenous medicine, translated into Latin by Juan Badiano. It is the earliest surviving illustrated work on Nahua medicine and botany.
milestones.explanation:
The Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco was founded to educate sons of the Nahua nobility. Martín de la Cruz, the college's Indigenous physician, set down remedies from Nahua medical knowledge, and Juan Badiano, a Nahua Latin teacher, translated them. The book, made for Francisco de Mendoza, son of the viceroy of New Spain, who sent it to Spain, contains some 185 painted plant illustrations alongside remedies.

The manuscript is unusual among sixteenth-century records of the Americas because it was written and translated by Indigenous authors rather than by European observers. Its blend of Nahua knowledge and European herbal form reflects the colonial setting in which it was made; the Nahuatl original has not survived.

The Latin manuscript spent nearly four centuries in European libraries, including the Vatican, where it was rediscovered in 1929. In 1990 Pope John Paul II returned it to Mexico, where it is held by the National Institute of Anthropology and History.

limitations: It was produced under colonial and missionary sponsorship, which shaped its form and content.

milestones.title: The Chamberlens' secret obstetric forceps
milestones.summary: Around 1600 a London family of surgeons and midwives, the Chamberlens, devised forceps that could deliver a living baby from an obstructed labour. They kept the design secret for over a century.
milestones.explanation:
Before forceps, an obstructed labour often ended with instruments that saved the mother only by destroying the child, or with the death of both. The Chamberlens, a Huguenot family settled in England, devised curved blades that could be applied separately around the baby's head and then joined, allowing a live birth.

The invention was probably made by Peter Chamberlen the elder and promoted by his nephew, Dr Peter Chamberlen. The family guarded it closely, working under blankets so that no one could see the instrument, and passed the secret down through four or five generations. Similar instruments were developed independently in Flanders and Holland, and forceps only became widely known in the early eighteenth century.

The original instruments were found in 1813 hidden at Woodham Mortimer Hall in Essex.

milestones.title: Fabrici describes the valves of the veins
milestones.summary: In 1603 Girolamo Fabrici (Fabricius ab Aquapendente), professor of anatomy at Padua, published De venarum ostiolis, the most detailed illustrated account of the valves in the veins to that date. He misread their purpose; his student William Harvey later used them as evidence that blood circulates.
milestones.explanation:
Valves inside the veins had been noticed by earlier anatomists, but Fabrici, professor of anatomy and surgery at Padua from 1565, examined them systematically. He demonstrated them in 1579 and in 1603 published a short illustrated treatise on them, De venarum ostiolis ('On the little doors of the veins'), printed in Padua.

He noted that the valves always point towards the heart. Following Galen, however, he believed that blood flowed outward through the veins, and explained the valves as brakes that stopped too much blood flowing back into the limbs, where the veins might burst.

William Harvey studied at Padua from 1598 to 1602, when Fabrici was at the height of his fame, and learned about the valves there. Harvey later explained them quite differently, as part of his theory of the circulation of the blood.

milestones.title: Harvey shows that the blood circulates
milestones.summary: In 1628 William Harvey, physician at St Bartholomew's Hospital in London, published De motu cordis, arguing from experiment and measurement that the heart pumps a fixed volume of blood around the body in a circuit.
milestones.explanation:
Harvey had studied at Padua and was appointed physician to St Bartholomew's Hospital in London in 1609. He investigated the movement of the blood by observation and experiment, working mostly on dogs and on cold-blooded animals such as frogs and snakes, whose slower hearts were easier to watch.

His decisive argument was quantitative. The heart pushes out so much blood with each beat that the body could not possibly make that amount anew, so a fixed volume of blood must go round and round, driven by the heart acting as a pump. He was already saying this at the end of his Lumleian lectures at the College of Physicians in 1616, but he published only in 1628, in a short Latin book printed in Frankfurt, then a centre of the European book trade.

The book was fiercely attacked; one critic called the idea paradoxical, useless, false, impossible, absurd and harmful. Harvey could not see how blood passed from the arteries to the veins and had to suppose that there were hidden connections. Marcello Malpighi observed the capillaries in 1661.

milestones.whyItMattered: Circulation became a foundation of physiology, and the book showed how experiment and measurement could overturn an ancient authority.

milestones.title: Cinchona bark enters medicine against fevers
milestones.summary: In the 1630s Jesuit missionaries in the Viceroyalty of Peru began using the bark of the Andean cinchona tree to treat intermittent fevers, and sent it to Europe. Its active ingredient, quinine, was isolated in Paris in 1820.
milestones.explanation:
The bark of cinchona trees, from the eastern slopes of the Andes, became known in Europe as 'Jesuits' bark' or 'Peruvian bark'. Jesuit missionaries were using it against fevers by about 1630, and shipments reached Europe in the following years, where it became the first effective treatment for malaria.

Popular stories credit its discovery to a feverish Indigenous man who drank water steeped with fallen cinchona, or to the cure of a Spanish countess. These are legends. Whether Andean peoples used the bark against fevers before European contact is uncertain.

Almost two centuries later, in 1820, the French pharmacists Pierre-Joseph Pelletier and Joseph Caventou isolated quinine from the bark. Purified quinine replaced the bark and allowed reliable dosing, decades before the malaria parasite itself was identified.

milestones.title: Hooke's Micrographia names the cell
milestones.summary: In 1665 Robert Hooke, curator of experiments to the Royal Society in London, published Micrographia, the first illustrated book of observations made with microscopes. Describing thin slices of cork, he called their tiny compartments 'cells'.
milestones.explanation:
Hooke built one of the best compound microscopes of his time, with its own lighting system, and used it in demonstrations at the Royal Society's weekly meetings, where he had been curator of experiments since 1662. Micrographia (1665) set out his observations with large engraved illustrations, including a famous flea, and became a best-seller.

In thin slices of cork he saw a honeycomb of small box-like spaces, which reminded him of the cells of a monastery, and he named them accordingly. What he saw were the walls of dead plant tissue. The word was later adopted for the basic unit of living things.

Antoni van Leeuwenhoek, who knew Hooke's work, built far more powerful microscopes and reported protozoa, bacteria, red blood cells and sperm cells in letters that the Royal Society translated and published.

milestones.whyItMattered: Microscopy went on to reveal micro-organisms and blood cells, and the cell became the basic unit of biology and of medicine's understanding of disease.
limitations: Hooke saw empty cell walls in dead cork, not living cells.

milestones.title: Boston's inoculation controversy and its numbers
milestones.summary: During Boston's 1721 smallpox epidemic, Zabdiel Boylston inoculated 282 people on the advice of Cotton Mather, who had learned of the practice from Onesimus. Boylston's counts suggested far lower mortality among the inoculated.
milestones.explanation:
When smallpox reached Boston in 1721, the minister Cotton Mather urged physicians to try inoculation. He had read reports from Constantinople in the Royal Society's journal and had heard about the practice from Onesimus, an African man he enslaved. Only one physician, Zabdiel Boylston, agreed.

The experiment provoked fury: inoculated people could spread smallpox, and critics mocked the practice for having been learned from Africans. Someone threw an explosive device through Mather's window. Boylston nonetheless kept records. Among 282 people he inoculated, 6 died (about 2%); among 5,759 residents who caught smallpox naturally and were not inoculated, 884 died (about 15%).

These numbers, together with comparable English figures collected by James Jurin, were among the earliest attempts to judge a medical practice by counting outcomes in comparable groups.

milestones.title: Amyand removes a perforated appendix
milestones.summary: In 1735 at St George's Hospital, London, the surgeon Claudius Amyand operated on an 11-year-old boy's hernia and found inside it an appendix perforated by a swallowed pin. He removed it: the earliest recorded successful appendicectomy.
milestones.explanation:
Hanvil Anderson, aged 11, was admitted to St George's Hospital at Hyde Park Corner with a scrotal hernia he had had since infancy and a fistula between the scrotum and thigh. When Amyand, the hospital's principal surgeon, opened the hernia he found the appendix inside it, pierced by a pin encrusted with stone. He removed the pin and the damaged appendix, and the operation succeeded.

Amyand described the case in a paper read to the Royal Society on 11 December 1735 and published in its Philosophical Transactions. It was an unplanned response to what he found, not a treatment for appendicitis, and the case fell into obscurity. Removing the appendix became an established operation only in the 1880s, after anaesthesia and antisepsis had made abdominal surgery far safer.

An appendix lying within an inguinal hernia is still called Amyand's hernia.

milestones.title: Lind compares six remedies for scurvy at sea
milestones.summary: On 20 May 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury, the naval surgeon James Lind gave twelve sailors with scurvy one of six treatments in pairs. The two given oranges and lemons recovered fastest.
milestones.explanation:
Scurvy killed huge numbers of sailors on long voyages. James Lind chose twelve men whose cases were as similar as he could find, kept them in the same part of the ship on the same diet, and assigned pairs to cider, elixir of vitriol, vinegar, sea water, oranges and lemons, or a purgative paste. Within six days one of the men given citrus was fit for duty, and the other was well enough to nurse the rest.

This deliberate comparison of treatments under similar conditions is one of the best-known early examples of a controlled clinical trial. Yet Lind's 1753 Treatise of the Scurvy did not single out citrus as a decisive cure, and its recommendations had little immediate impact. The Royal Navy did not issue citrus juice routinely until 1795, more than four decades later.

milestones.title: Priestley isolates oxygen at Bowood
milestones.summary: On 1 August 1774, in the Earl of Shelburne's laboratory at Bowood House in Wiltshire, Joseph Priestley heated red mercuric oxide and collected a new gas. He called it 'dephlogisticated air'; Lavoisier named it oxygen.
milestones.explanation:
Priestley, a dissenting minister and teacher, investigated gases ('airs') from the early 1770s and described several new ones, among them nitrous oxide. In 1773 he became librarian and companion to the Earl of Shelburne, whose estate at Bowood gave him a laboratory. There, on 1 August 1774, he heated red mercuric oxide and isolated a new air.

He interpreted it through the then-dominant phlogiston theory of burning and called it 'dephlogisticated air'. Later that year, in Paris, he told Antoine Lavoisier about it. Lavoisier recognised it as part of the atmosphere, named it oxygen and used it to overturn the phlogiston theory. Priestley never accepted the new chemistry.

The Swedish apothecary Carl Wilhelm Scheele prepared the same gas, probably earlier, but published later.

milestones.title: Withering's account of the foxglove
milestones.summary: In 1785 William Withering, physician to the General Hospital in Birmingham, published An Account of the Foxglove: 163 patients with dropsy treated with foxglove leaf, reported whether they did well or not, with a clear description of the drug's dangerous side effects.
milestones.explanation:
Foxglove had been known to herbalists for centuries. Withering, who joined the staff of Birmingham's General Hospital in 1775, was asked about a family remedy for dropsy kept secret by an old woman in Shropshire. The mixture contained at least twenty herbs, and he concluded that the active one could be no other than the foxglove.

Over about ten years he tried different preparations, found dried, powdered leaf more reliable than fresh leaf or a decoction, and learned to adjust the dose. His book reports 163 cases. He chose to include every patient he had treated, whether the outcome was good or bad, because a selection of successes would have misled his readers. He described the toxic effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and disturbed, green-yellow vision) and advised stopping and restarting at a lower dose when they appeared.

He did not know how foxglove worked. He thought mainly of its effect on urine, though he noticed that it could calm a disordered heartbeat. Other physicians later used it in excessive doses or where it could not help.

milestones.title: Desault's clinical school and surgical journal
milestones.summary: At the Hôtel-Dieu in Paris, the surgeon Pierre-Joseph Desault built a clinical school that taught surgery at the bedside, in French, to students from across Europe. In 1791 he founded the Journal de chirurgie to record the most instructive cases from his wards.
milestones.explanation:
Desault, born in Franche-Comté and trained partly in a military hospital, opened a school of anatomy in Paris in 1766 that drew around 300 pupils, to the resentment of established teachers. After posts at the Charité hospital, he took charge of surgery at the Hôtel-Dieu, Paris's main public hospital, in the mid-1780s.

There he organised teaching around patients: students followed cases on the wards and watched and practised procedures, with lectures given in French rather than Latin. In 1791 he founded the Journal de chirurgie, edited by his pupils, which published the most interesting cases from his clinical school together with his comments on them.

His students, among them Xavier Bichat, spread his methods; much of what is known of his teaching comes from their publications after his death in 1795.

milestones.title: Hahnemann founds homeopathy
milestones.summary: In 1796 the German physician Samuel Hahnemann published the principle that 'like cures like', drawn from taking cinchona bark himself in 1790. Homeopathy spread widely in the nineteenth century; reviews of the evidence have found no health condition for which it reliably works.
milestones.explanation:
Hahnemann was critical of the medicine of his day. In 1790, living near Leipzig and translating the Scottish physician William Cullen's Materia Medica, he rejected Cullen's explanation of why cinchona bark helped against malarial fevers and took the bark himself for several days. He reported symptoms resembling the fever, and concluded that a substance which causes symptoms in a healthy person can cure similar symptoms in someone who is ill.

He first published this 'principle of similars' in 1796, in a German journal of practical medicine, and in 1810 set out his system in the Organon. Homeopathic remedies came to be given in extremely diluted forms. By the late nineteenth century homeopathy was practised in more than 30 countries, with its own medical schools and hospitals, and it remains popular in parts of Europe and in India.

Its principles have not stood up to testing. In 2015 Australia's National Health and Medical Research Council concluded, after assessing the published systematic reviews, that there are no health conditions for which there is reliable evidence that homeopathy is effective.

milestones.title: Jenner tests cowpox as protection against smallpox
milestones.summary: On 14 May 1796 Edward Jenner inoculated eight-year-old James Phipps with material from a milkmaid's cowpox sore, then showed the boy did not react to smallpox. His 1798 publication launched vaccination.
milestones.explanation:
Country people had long observed that milkmaids who caught cowpox, a mild disease, seemed to escape smallpox. Edward Jenner, a physician in Berkeley, Gloucestershire, set out to test the idea. On 14 May 1796 he took material from a cowpox lesion on the hand of a milkmaid, Sarah Nelmes, and inoculated James Phipps, the son of his gardener. Six weeks later he inoculated the boy with smallpox material, and no disease followed.

Jenner gathered further cases and published An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae in 1798. Vaccination, from the Latin for cow, was safer than variolation because it did not produce smallpox and could not spread it. Within a few years it was being carried around the world.

Jenner was not the first to try cowpox deliberately: in 1774 the Dorset farmer Benjamin Jesty had inoculated his wife and two sons with cowpox during a smallpox outbreak. Jenner's contribution was systematic testing and publication.

milestones.title: Davy suggests nitrous oxide against surgical pain
milestones.summary: Experimenting at the Medical Pneumatic Institution in Bristol, the young chemist Humphry Davy inhaled nitrous oxide repeatedly and in 1800 noted that, as it seemed capable of destroying physical pain, it might be used during surgical operations. The idea lay unused for over 40 years.
milestones.explanation:
The physician Thomas Beddoes opened the Pneumatic Institution at Clifton, Bristol, in 1798 to treat diseases such as consumption with inhaled gases, and hired Davy, then 19, to run its research. Rejecting the belief that nitrous oxide was deadly to breathe, Davy inhaled it many times, recording its effects on himself and on friends.

In 1800 he published a 580-page account of the work. Near the end, almost in passing, he remarked that because nitrous oxide appeared capable of destroying physical pain, it might probably be used with advantage during surgical operations in which there was little bleeding.

Nobody followed this up. The gas became known as laughing gas, and its use against surgical pain was not pursued until the 1840s. In January 1845 the dentist Horace Wells tried to demonstrate it at Massachusetts General Hospital; the patient groaned and moved, and the demonstration was judged a failure.

milestones.whatChanged: Showed that nitrous oxide could be breathed safely and recorded that it relieved pain.
milestones.whyItMattered: Nitrous oxide later became one of the first anaesthetic gases; the long gap before anyone acted on Davy's remark shows that an observation alone does not change practice.
limitations: Davy's remark was a passing comment, and historians differ on how much he was concerned with surgical pain.
Nitrous oxide on its own gives a lighter state of unconsciousness than ether, which helps explain Wells's failure in 1845.

milestones.title: Sertürner isolates morphine from opium
milestones.summary: Between 1803 and 1805 Friedrich Sertürner, a young pharmacist's assistant in Paderborn, isolated the sleep-inducing substance in opium. Named morphium after the god of dreams, it was the first alkaloid obtained from any plant.
milestones.explanation:
Sertürner trained at the court pharmacy in Paderborn. Just after finishing his apprenticeship he set out to find the substance responsible for opium's effects, and found that adding ammonia to a clarified opium extract separated an almost pure material. He first reported it in 1805 in a letter to a pharmaceutical journal, and soon described it as a weak base, which he called morphium.

The work drew little notice until 1817, when he published a full account of its isolation, crystallisation, chemistry and effects, tested on rats, dogs, himself and others. Small doses produced light-headed, happy feelings; larger ones caused drowsiness, exhaustion and confusion. He suggested it was the first of a new class of 'vegetable alkalis', and the word alkaloid was coined the following year.

A pure active ingredient could now be given in measured doses instead of crude opium. Commercial production began in 1827 at a pharmacy in Darmstadt that became the firm Merck.

milestones.whyItMattered: Morphine became a mainstay of pain relief, and Sertürner's work showed that the active substance of a medicinal plant could be isolated and studied as a pure chemical.
limitations: Acidic substances had been extracted from plants before; morphine was the first plant base, later called an alkaloid, to be isolated and recognised as such.

milestones.title: The Balmis expedition carries vaccine across two oceans
milestones.summary: From 1803 a Spanish royal expedition led by Francisco Xavier de Balmis carried smallpox vaccine to the Americas and Asia, keeping it alive by passing it arm to arm through a chain of orphaned children.
milestones.explanation:
Cowpox material lost its potency within days, so it could not survive a long voyage in a bottle. Balmis's solution was to take children who had never had smallpox and vaccinate them in sequence: as one child's pustule matured, fluid from it was used to vaccinate the next.

The expedition sailed from La Coruña on 30 November 1803 with 22 boys from an orphanage in Santiago de Compostela. In the Americas it divided. José Salvany led a branch through present-day Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia and Chile, a journey that lasted years, while Balmis took the vaccine to New Spain. There he recruited further children to carry it across the Pacific to the Philippines, and from there it reached Macao.

The expedition is often described as the first international, philanthropic vaccination campaign.

date.basis: Commonly dated 1803–1806 for Balmis's own route, from the departure from La Coruña on 30 November 1803. Salvany's branch continued in South America for several more years; sources give end dates between 1806 and 1814.

milestones.title: Hanaoka Seishū operates under general anaesthesia
milestones.summary: On 13 October 1804 the surgeon Hanaoka Seishū gave a 60-year-old woman, Kan Aiya, an oral herbal anaesthetic, tsūsensan, and removed a breast tumour while she was unconscious.
milestones.explanation:
Hanaoka Seishū (1760–1835) practised in Kii Province, combining Chinese-derived herbal medicine with surgical ideas reaching Japan through Dutch books. He spent years developing tsūsensan (also called mafutsusan), a drink based mainly on Datura and other plants, testing it on animals and, according to biographers, on members of his own family.

On 13 October 1804 he used it to anaesthetise Kan Aiya and excised her breast cancer. This is the earliest well-documented operation under general anaesthesia, more than four decades before ether was demonstrated in the United States. Hanaoka went on to perform many more operations with the drug and trained numerous students.

Because Japan's contacts with the outside world were tightly restricted at the time, his work was little known abroad and did not influence the later development of ether and chloroform anaesthesia in Europe and North America. The two lines developed independently.

date.basis: Date recorded in Hanaoka's case record and repeated in scholarly accounts.

milestones.whatChanged: Demonstrated that a patient could be rendered unconscious for major surgery with a reproducible preparation.
milestones.whyItMattered: Showed that surgical anaesthesia was achievable decades before ether, and illustrates parallel, unconnected routes to the same goal.
limitations: Tsūsensan's main active ingredients are toxic anticholinergic alkaloids; it was not a safe anaesthetic by modern standards.
Who transcribed the surviving case manuscript has been questioned by historians.

milestones.title: Laennec invents the stethoscope
milestones.summary: In 1816 at the Necker Hospital in Paris, René Laennec rolled paper into a tube to listen to a patient's chest, then built a wooden stethoscope. His 1819 treatise linked the sounds he heard to findings at autopsy.
milestones.explanation:
Physicians sometimes listened to the chest by pressing an ear against it, which was awkward and often uninformative. According to the best-known account, Laennec was examining a young woman with suspected heart disease when he rolled a sheaf of paper into a tube and found that heart and breath sounds were much clearer through it. He soon replaced the paper with a wooden cylinder.

Laennec's real innovation was method. He systematically compared the sounds heard through the instrument with what he later found at post-mortem examination, building a vocabulary of signs such as rales and egophony. He set this out in De l'auscultation médiate (1819), which taught a generation of students from many countries.

Accounts differ on the date of the first use: some give February 1816, others 13 September 1816.

milestones.title: Blundell transfuses human blood
milestones.summary: From 1818 the London obstetrician James Blundell, determined to save women bleeding to death after childbirth, carried out the first documented transfusions of human blood into patients. His first patient died; in 1829 he published a case in which a woman with severe bleeding after childbirth recovered.
milestones.explanation:
Blundell, an obstetrician at Guy's Hospital, was, in his own words, appalled at his helplessness in the face of fatal haemorrhage during delivery. He experimented on dogs and, following the Edinburgh graduate John Leacock, who had argued that blood from another species was harmful, concluded that only human blood should be used.

In 1818 he transfused blood from several donors into a man dying of stomach cancer, who improved briefly but died two days later. Between 1818 and 1829 Blundell and his colleagues performed ten transfusions; at most four succeeded, and some patients were probably already dead. In 1829 The Lancet published a case in which a woman with severe bleeding after childbirth recovered after receiving eight ounces of blood, given gradually over three hours.

Blundell designed instruments for transfusion and promoted it widely, always crediting Leacock's earlier work. Without knowledge of blood groups, discovered almost a century later, transfusion remained risky and unpredictable.

milestones.title: Ether anaesthesia: a country practice and a public demonstration
milestones.summary: Crawford Long used ether during surgery in Jefferson, Georgia, in March 1842 but did not publicise it. On 16 October 1846 William Morton's public demonstration at Massachusetts General Hospital spread surgical anaesthesia around the world.
milestones.explanation:
The intoxicating effects of inhaled ether had been known for centuries. On 30 March 1842, Crawford Long, a physician in rural Georgia, etherised a patient, James Venable, to remove cysts from his neck, and went on to use ether in other operations. He did not report this promptly, so his work had no immediate influence.

On 16 October 1846, the Boston dentist William T. G. Morton administered sulphuric ether to Edward Gilbert Abbott in the surgical amphitheatre of Massachusetts General Hospital, now called the Ether Dome, while the surgeon John Collins Warren operated on a lesion under Abbott's jaw. Hospital records show the operation was a ligation of the lesion's blood supply rather than the tumour excision often described. The technique was quickly adopted around the world.

The demonstration was followed by twenty years of bitter dispute over credit between Morton, the chemist Charles Jackson and the dentist Horace Wells, none of whom had been first. Morton also tried to patent ether.

milestones.whyItMattered: Anaesthesia allowed longer, more careful operations and transformed surgery and dentistry.

milestones.title: Leukaemia recognised as a disease of the blood
milestones.summary: In 1845 John Hughes Bennett in Edinburgh, and six weeks later Rudolf Virchow in Germany, independently described patients whose blood was overwhelmed by white cells. Virchow called it 'white blood', and later leukämie.
milestones.explanation:
In March 1845 a slater named John Monteith died at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, where he had been under the care of Robert Christison, with a hugely enlarged spleen and liver. John Hughes Bennett examined the body and found the blood full of what he took to be pus cells, without any source of infection. He published the case later that year as one in which death came from 'suppuration of the blood'.

Six weeks after Bennett's report, Virchow, a young pathologist in Berlin, independently published a similar post-mortem case. Rather than calling it infection, he argued that the blood itself was abnormal, called the condition 'white blood' (weisses Blut) and two years later coined the name leukämie, from the Greek for white and blood.

The two men disputed priority for some years. Virchow eventually acknowledged Bennett's earlier publication.

date.basis: Both reports were published in 1845, Virchow's about six weeks after Bennett's. The name leukämie dates from 1847.

milestones.title: Sims's fistula operations on enslaved women
milestones.summary: From 1845 to 1849, in a small hospital behind his house in Montgomery, Alabama, J. Marion Sims repeatedly operated without anaesthesia on enslaved women with vesicovaginal fistulas until he found a repair that worked. Three of the women are known by name: Anarcha, Betsey and Lucy.
milestones.explanation:
A vesicovaginal fistula, a hole between the bladder and vagina left by prolonged obstructed labour, caused constant leaking of urine and was generally considered incurable. Sims, a physician who treated enslaved people on plantations around Montgomery, devised a speculum that let him see the injury clearly and began experimental operations in late 1845.

About a dozen enslaved women, placed in his care by the people who enslaved them, were operated on over four years. Anarcha, aged 17, underwent 30 operations before her fistula closed in 1849. Sims never used anaesthesia in these operations, even after ether became available in 1846. The women also served as his nurses and surgical assistants once his colleagues stopped attending. No account by any of them survives.

Sims's success made his reputation, and he became one of the most celebrated surgeons of the nineteenth century, often called the father of modern gynaecology.

milestones.whatChanged: Produced the first consistently successful operation for vesicovaginal fistula.
milestones.whyItMattered: The repair relieved a devastating injury of childbirth, but the way it was developed has become a central case in debates about consent, race and exploitation in medicine.
limitations: Almost everything known comes from Sims's own writings; the women's experience is unrecorded.
milestones.contested: Historians and ethicists disagree about how to judge Sims. L. L. Wall has argued from the historical record that the operations were therapeutic, that the women wanted their fistulas repaired and cooperated, and that the charges against Sims are largely without merit. Critics argue that enslaved women could not meaningfully refuse, and point to Sims's own account of their pain. In 2018 New York City moved his statue from Central Park; in 2021 a monument to the 'Mothers of Gynecology' was unveiled in Montgomery.

They underwent repeated painful operations without anaesthesia, often naked and watched by other physicians, at a time when many white doctors, Sims included, believed that Black people felt less pain.

milestones.title: Semmelweis orders hand disinfection on a maternity ward
milestones.summary: In May 1847, at Vienna's General Hospital, Ignaz Semmelweis required doctors and medical students to wash their hands in chlorinated lime before examining women in labour. Deaths from puerperal fever fell sharply.
milestones.explanation:
Vienna's maternity hospital had two clinics, and women were admitted to them on alternate days. From 1840 to 1846, about 98 of every 1,000 mothers died in the first clinic, where doctors and medical students worked, against about 36 per 1,000 in the second, staffed by midwives. Almost all the deaths were from puerperal (childbed) fever.

Semmelweis concluded that students and doctors were carrying 'cadaverous particles' on their hands from the autopsy room to the delivery ward. From 15 May 1847 he required everyone to scrub with a chlorinated lime solution until the smell of the dissecting room was gone. Mortality in the first clinic fell to around the level of the midwives' clinic, and rose again after he left Vienna in 1850 and the practice lapsed.

His ideas were resisted, and he was slow to publish: students and colleagues reported his findings, and his own book appeared only in 1861. Germ theory, which explained why handwashing worked, came later.

milestones.whyItMattered: Hand hygiene is now the cornerstone of infection prevention in health care.
