milestones.title: Women begin to earn medical degrees in the United States
milestones.summary: In 1849 Elizabeth Blackwell became the first woman to receive an MD from an American medical school. In 1850 Quakers in Philadelphia founded the Female Medical College of Pennsylvania, the first medical school in the world for women authorised to award the MD.
milestones.explanation:
Women had long practised medicine as healers, nurses and midwives, but were barred from formal training as physicians. Elizabeth Blackwell, born in Bristol, England, applied to many medical schools before Geneva Medical College in western New York accepted her in 1847. On 23 January 1849 she received her degree in the town's Presbyterian church. She went on to support medical education for women in the United States and Britain.

In 1850, two years after the women's rights convention at Seneca Falls, a group of progressive physicians and laymen, most of them Quakers, chartered the Female Medical College of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia. It opened that year on Arch Street, and its first graduates, in 1851, included Ann Preston, who later became the first woman dean of an American medical school. The college, renamed the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania in 1867, trained thousands of women physicians who practised around the world.

Opposition was fierce, and women students were openly harassed.

milestones.title: John Snow traces a cholera outbreak to a water pump
milestones.summary: During the Soho cholera outbreak of 1854, John Snow gathered evidence that cases were linked to water from the Broad Street pump and persuaded local officials to remove its handle on 8 September.
milestones.explanation:
Many physicians at the time believed cholera spread through foul air, or miasma. John Snow, a London physician also known for his work on anaesthesia, argued that it was spread by something taken in by mouth, most likely in water.

When a severe outbreak struck Soho at the end of August 1854, killing more than 600 people, Snow examined the addresses of the dead and interviewed residents. Deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump, and telling exceptions fitted his theory: workers at a nearby brewery who drank beer escaped, while a woman living far away who had Broad Street water brought to her daily died. He presented his evidence to the parish board of guardians, and the pump handle was removed the next day, 8 September.

The outbreak was already declining by then, and the famous map of deaths was drawn afterwards to present the case rather than to discover it. Snow's broader argument that cholera is waterborne was not widely accepted in his lifetime.

milestones.title: Virchow's Cellular Pathology
milestones.summary: In 1858 Rudolf Virchow published his Berlin lectures as Die Cellularpathologie, arguing that disease is a disturbance of the body's cells and that every cell arises from another cell. The idea displaced the ancient theory of imbalanced humours.
milestones.explanation:
Virchow trained in Berlin, held the first chair of pathological anatomy in Germany at Würzburg from 1849, and was recalled to Berlin in 1856 to lead its Pathological Institute. Early in 1858 he gave a series of 20 lectures there, published the same year as Cellular Pathology as Based upon Physiological and Pathological Histology.

Building on the recent theory that plants and animals are made of cells, Virchow argued that the cell is the basic unit of life and of disease: illnesses arise from changes in particular cells and tissues, and every cell comes from a pre-existing cell (omnis cellula e cellula). Disease, on this view, was to be found by examining tissues under the microscope, not by reasoning about imbalances of bodily fluids.

Virchow was also active in politics and public health; Berlin's modern sewer system owes much to him.

milestones.title: Pasteur's swan-neck flasks and the germ theory
milestones.summary: Between 1859 and 1862 Louis Pasteur showed in Paris that boiled broth stays sterile in a flask whose curved neck traps airborne dust, and spoils only when microbes from the air reach it. The work undermined spontaneous generation and supported the germ theory of disease.
milestones.explanation:
Many scientists still believed that microbes could arise spontaneously in decaying matter. Pasteur, whose work on fermentation had convinced him that it was caused by living micro-organisms, set out in 1859 to settle the question by experiment.

He boiled a nutrient liquid in a flask whose long neck he had drawn out into a downward S-curve, then let it cool. Air could still enter, but dust and germs settled in the bend of the neck, and the liquid stayed unaltered. Once the neck was broken, microbes soon grew in it. In 1862, after a public dispute with Félix Pouchet, a leading defender of spontaneous generation, he published his results.

Pasteur concluded that microbes are everywhere, in water, in air and on objects and skin, and that some of them cause disease. The idea underpinned Lister's antiseptic surgery and the later identification of specific disease-causing bacteria.

milestones.title: Snellen's eye chart
milestones.summary: In 1862 Herman Snellen of the Netherlands Hospital for Eye Patients in Utrecht published his optotypes: letters of graded sizes, each built on a 5 × 5 grid, for measuring sharpness of vision. Versions of his chart remain in use worldwide.
milestones.explanation:
Earlier tests, such as Eduard Jäger's reading-type cards, measured how well people could read ordinary print of various sizes. Snellen, assistant and then first physician at the eye hospital founded in Utrecht by Franciscus Donders, chose not to use existing typefaces. He designed special letters, which he called optotypes, each drawn within a square divided into 5 × 5 parts, so that the detail of each letter had a defined size.

Visual acuity could then be expressed as a fraction: the distance at which the person reads a line, over the distance at which a normal eye can just read it. He published the charts in 1862.

Snellen later became professor of ophthalmology at Utrecht in 1877 and director of the eye hospital in 1884.

milestones.title: Lister treats a compound fracture with carbolic acid
milestones.summary: On 12 August 1865 at Glasgow Royal Infirmary, Joseph Lister dressed the open leg fracture of a boy, James Greenlees, with carbolic acid. The wound healed without infection, and Lister published the method in 1867.
milestones.explanation:
Compound fractures, where broken bone pierces the skin, frequently became infected and could lead to amputation or death. Lister, Regius Professor of Surgery at Glasgow, had read Louis Pasteur's work on microorganisms and reasoned that something entering the wound from outside caused the putrefaction.

When James Greenlees was brought in after being run over by a cart, Lister set the bone and dressed the wound with carbolic acid (phenol). The boy recovered fully. Lister treated further cases and in 1867 published a series of articles in The Lancet setting out what he called the antiseptic principle.

He later extended the approach to the surgical environment as a whole, using a carbolic spray during his years in Edinburgh.

milestones.title: Ellis Shipp's school of obstetrics and nursing, Utah
milestones.summary: After graduating from the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania in March 1878, Ellis Reynolds Shipp returned to Salt Lake City and opened a school of obstetrics and nursing. Over five decades it trained about 500 women as midwives and nurses across Utah.
milestones.explanation:
Leaders of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, concerned about deaths of mothers and infants in Utah Territory, encouraged women to train as physicians in the East. Shipp took the place of a homesick sister wife at the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania and graduated on 14 March 1878.

Back in Salt Lake City she set up a practice in obstetrics and women's diseases and, realising that a few women doctors could not meet the need, opened a school to train midwives and nurses, advertised with free scholarships. Its graduates became licensed midwives in communities throughout the territory. Shipp herself is said to have delivered more than 5,000 babies, and she helped found the Deseret Hospital.

milestones.title: A caesarean delivery observed in Bunyoro
milestones.summary: In 1879 a visiting medical student, Robert Felkin, watched practitioners in the kingdom of Bunyoro deliver a baby by caesarean section. Mother and child were alive when he left 11 days later.
milestones.explanation:
Robert Felkin was travelling with a missionary party in the Great Lakes region when, at a place he called Kahura, he witnessed a caesarean section carried out by a local surgeon and assistants. His account was presented to the Edinburgh Obstetrical Society in 1884.

According to Felkin, the patient, a young woman in her first pregnancy, was made half-intoxicated with banana wine, which was also used to wash the surgeon's hands and her abdomen. The surgeon opened the abdomen and uterus, delivered the baby, cleared the uterus of clots and the placenta, and closed the wound by pinning the edges together with iron spikes, covered with clean cloth. Felkin followed the mother and baby for 11 days and both did well.

Felkin concluded that the operation was well established. At the time, caesarean section in European hospitals still carried a very high maternal death rate, which makes the account notable, though it cannot be generalised from a single case.

milestones.title: Pasteur's attenuated vaccines: chicken cholera and anthrax
milestones.summary: In 1879 Louis Pasteur's laboratory found that ageing cultures of the chicken cholera bacterium lost their virulence yet protected chickens. In May 1881 a public trial at Pouilly-le-Fort showed that an attenuated anthrax vaccine protected sheep, cattle and a goat.
milestones.explanation:
Inspired by Jenner, Pasteur hoped that vaccines could be found for all infectious diseases. In 1879 chickens inoculated with an old culture of the chicken cholera bacterium, left standing for weeks, became only mildly ill and then resisted fresh, virulent bacteria. Pasteur called this weakening 'attenuation' and attributed it to exposure to oxygen.

With Charles Chamberland and Émile Roux he then developed an anthrax vaccine. At a farm at Pouilly-le-Fort, near Paris, 24 sheep, a goat and six cows were vaccinated twice in May 1881 while a similar group was not. On 31 May all were injected with virulent anthrax. By 2 June the vaccinated animals were healthy, while the unvaccinated sheep and goat were dead and the unvaccinated cows ill. The trial, held before journalists and officials, made Pasteur's vaccine famous.

Chamberland's private notebooks, studied much later, show that the vaccine used at Pouilly-le-Fort had been weakened with potassium dichromate, a method close to that of Pasteur's rival Jean-Joseph Henri Toussaint, rather than by oxygen as Pasteur's public account implied.

milestones.title: Laveran sees the malaria parasite in a soldier's blood
milestones.summary: On 6 November 1880, at the military hospital in Constantine, the French army physician Alphonse Laveran saw moving parasites in the fresh blood of a soldier with malaria.
milestones.explanation:
Laveran had been posted to French military hospitals in Algeria, where malaria was common and often severe. Studying the dark pigment found in the blood of patients, he noticed unfamiliar bodies, and on 6 November 1880 at Constantine he watched one put out moving filaments, a sign that it was alive. He concluded that malaria was caused by a parasite, not a bacterium or a miasma.

He reported the finding to the French Academy of Medicine in November 1880. Many colleagues were sceptical, partly because others were searching for a 'malaria bacillus'; recognition came only gradually, by about 1889.

It was the first protozoan shown to cause an infectious disease, and it opened the way to the work on how malaria spreads.

milestones.whatChanged: Identified a parasite in human blood as the cause of malaria, overturning bacterial and 'bad air' explanations.
milestones.whyItMattered: Made diagnosis by microscopy possible and set up the search for how the parasite reaches people.
limitations: Laveran's observation was not widely accepted for about a decade.
The full life cycle, including transmission by mosquitoes, was worked out by others later.

milestones.title: Koch identifies the cause of tuberculosis
milestones.summary: On 24 March 1882, at the Berlin Physiological Society, Robert Koch announced that he had found the bacterium that causes tuberculosis, then responsible for about one in seven deaths in Europe and the United States.
milestones.explanation:
Tuberculosis was widely thought to be hereditary or constitutional. Using new staining methods and culture media, Koch showed rod-shaped bacteria in tuberculous tissue from humans and animals, grew them in pure culture on blood serum, and reproduced the disease by inoculating animals with the cultures.

He presented his findings in a lecture on the aetiology of tuberculosis and published them three weeks later. In 1884 he set out the criteria, now called Koch's postulates, for linking a specific microbe to a specific disease, which became a foundation of bacteriology.

Identifying the cause did not immediately produce a cure; effective drugs arrived only in the 1940s. The anniversary of Koch's lecture has been observed as World TB Day since 1982.

milestones.whyItMattered: Established methods for identifying the causes of infectious diseases and redirected tuberculosis control towards preventing transmission.
limitations: Knowing the cause did not by itself provide a treatment; effective antibiotics came some sixty years later.

milestones.title: Rabies vaccine given to Joseph Meister
milestones.summary: On 6 July 1885 in Paris, nine-year-old Joseph Meister, bitten 14 times by a rabid dog, began a course of injections of dried rabid spinal cord prepared in Louis Pasteur's laboratory. He never developed rabies, and the success led to the founding of the Institut Pasteur.
milestones.explanation:
Rabies was invariably fatal once symptoms appeared, but its long incubation offered time to act after a bite. Pasteur's team had weakened the rabies agent by air-drying the spinal cords of infected rabbits, and reported protecting dogs.

Meister's mother brought him from Alsace to Paris. Pasteur was not a physician, so Dr Jacques-Joseph Grancher gave the injections: 13 over about ten days, each made from progressively fresher, more virulent cord. Meister stayed well. In October a shepherd, Jean-Baptiste Jupille, was treated, and by March 1886 Pasteur reported results for 350 people. The flood of patients prompted the Academy of Sciences to call for a rabies vaccine centre, and the Institut Pasteur opened in 1888.

Pasteur's private notebooks, kept by his family until the 1970s, complicate the story. They record that he had treated two people before Meister, one of whom died, and that the preparation Meister received had been made by methods little tested in animals.

milestones.whyItMattered: Post-exposure rabies vaccination still saves lives, and the demand it created founded the Institut Pasteur, a model for research institutes worldwide.
limitations: Not everyone bitten by a rabid animal develops rabies, so a single survivor could not prove the treatment worked; there was no control group.

milestones.title: Recording the heart's electrical activity
milestones.summary: In May 1887 Augustus Waller recorded the first electrocardiogram from a human heart at St Mary's Hospital, London. Willem Einthoven, who saw Waller's demonstrations, built a far more sensitive string galvanometer at Leiden and by 1903 was recording clear, clinically useful ECGs.
milestones.explanation:
Waller used a capillary electrometer, in which a mercury column moves slightly with electric current, and photographed the shadow of the moving meniscus on a travelling plate. His 1887 tracings from the intact human heart showed only two distorted deflections, and he doubted that the method would ever be much use in hospitals.

Einthoven, professor of physiology at Leiden, first corrected the distortions of the capillary electrometer mathematically and named the deflections P, Q, R, S and T. He then developed a string galvanometer, a fine silver-coated quartz thread stretched between the poles of a strong magnet, which he described in 1901 and used to publish detailed ECGs in 1903.

It made the electrocardiogram a practical tool for detecting heart disease. Einthoven received the 1924 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

milestones.title: Antitoxin serum against diphtheria and tetanus
milestones.summary: In 1890, Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburō, working in Robert Koch's institute in Berlin, showed that serum from immunised animals could neutralise diphtheria and tetanus toxins and protect other animals. Serum therapy followed.
milestones.explanation:
Diphtheria killed large numbers of children by producing a toxin. Behring and Kitasato found that animals injected with the toxins of diphtheria or tetanus bacteria produced substances in their blood that neutralised them. Serum taken from such animals could protect untreated animals and even cure sick ones. They published their findings jointly in 1890.

Behring concluded that immunity could be transferred in the blood, an idea now called passive immunisation. Horse serum against diphtheria was soon tested in children, with an early report on 30 bacteriologically confirmed cases in 1893, and antitoxin was used in hospitals to reduce deaths during outbreaks by the mid-1890s. Similar work was under way in France at almost the same time.

The first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, in 1901, went to Behring alone for serum therapy, although the foundational 1890 paper was co-authored with Kitasato.

milestones.title: Röntgen discovers X-rays
milestones.summary: On 8 November 1895 at the University of Würzburg, Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen noticed a fluorescent screen glowing near a shielded cathode-ray tube. He identified a new, penetrating radiation he called X-rays.
milestones.explanation:
Röntgen was experimenting with cathode-ray tubes when a fluorescent screen in his laboratory began to glow for no apparent reason. After weeks of work, often eating and sleeping in the laboratory, he showed that the tube emitted invisible rays able to pass through materials that were opaque to ordinary light. Because their nature was unknown, he called them X-rays.

He mailed his first announcement to colleagues on 1 January 1896, and the news spread around the world through the press. The discovery very soon made an impact on practical medicine, letting doctors see inside the body without surgery. Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

milestones.title: Mosquitoes shown to carry malaria
milestones.summary: In 1897 Ronald Ross found malaria parasites developing in the stomach of an Anopheles mosquito that had fed on a patient. Over the next three years, Battista Grassi's team in Rome showed how human malaria is transmitted.
milestones.explanation:
Patrick Manson and Laveran had suggested that mosquitoes might spread malaria. Ronald Ross, an officer in the Indian Medical Service, spent more than two years dissecting mosquitoes before, on 20 August 1897 at Secunderabad, he found pigmented cysts in the stomach wall of an anopheline mosquito fed on a patient with malaria. He then worked out the full transmission cycle using a malaria parasite of birds.

In Italy, Giovanni Battista Grassi and colleagues showed that human malaria is transmitted specifically by Anopheles mosquitoes, confirming the cycle in humans by about 1900. Ross and Grassi quarrelled bitterly over priority; the 1902 Nobel Prize went to Ross alone.

Knowing the vector made it possible to attack malaria by controlling mosquitoes and their breeding sites, alongside treating the infection.

milestones.title: Insulin first treats a dying boy in Toronto
milestones.summary: In 1921–22 a University of Toronto team extracted insulin from the pancreas. On 23 January 1922 a purified extract brought 14-year-old Leonard Thompson's diabetes under control, turning a fatal disease into a treatable one.
milestones.explanation:
Type 1 diabetes was then a universally fatal disease. In the summer of 1921 Frederick Banting and Charles Best, working in J. J. R. Macleod's laboratory, showed that a pancreatic extract lowered blood sugar in diabetic dogs. Early presentations did not convince everyone, since earlier investigators had reported similar effects without producing a usable treatment.

On 11 January 1922 Leonard Thompson, a 14-year-old near death at Toronto General Hospital, was injected with Banting and Best's extract. It lowered his blood sugar but had little clinical effect. The biochemist James Collip then produced a purer extract, and from 23 January Thompson improved dramatically. He lived another 13 years.

Production was scaled up with the university's Connaught Laboratories and drug companies, and the Nobel Prize of 1923 went to two members of the team, Banting and Macleod, amid lasting disputes over credit.

milestones.title: Penicillin: from a mould in London to mass production
milestones.summary: Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a Penicillium mould killed bacteria. A decade later Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their Oxford team showed it could treat infections, and wartime research in the United States made mass production possible.
milestones.explanation:
Returning from holiday in September 1928, Fleming found a culture plate at St Mary's Hospital in London where bacteria had failed to grow around a contaminating mould. He identified it as Penicillium and showed it killed many disease-causing bacteria, but the substance was hard to produce and remained a laboratory curiosity.

From 1939, Florey, Chain, Norman Heatley and others at Oxford developed ways to extract it and showed that it protected infected mice. In 1941 an Oxford police constable became the first person treated; he improved but died when supplies ran out.

With Britain at war, production research moved to the United States, including the Department of Agriculture laboratory in Peoria, Illinois, and drug companies that developed deep-tank fermentation. Penicillin was produced at scale from 1944. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize.

milestones.title: Mapping the brain's electrical activity across the scalp
milestones.summary: William Grey Walter used EEG with many small scalp electrodes to locate a brain tumour in 1936, and at the Burden Neurological Institute in Bristol in 1957 built the toposcope, which displayed brain electrical activity from many points at once.
milestones.explanation:
Hans Berger's electrodes were too large to show where in the brain activity came from. Working in London in 1936, Grey Walter showed that with many small electrodes and triangulation he could locate abnormal slow waves and so detect a cerebral tumour. Moving to the new Burden Neurological Institute in Bristol in 1939, he built a series of instruments to analyse the EEG.

His toposcope of 1957 arranged display tubes in a two-dimensional array matching the electrodes on the head, so that changing patterns of activity could be watched across the brain's surface.

milestones.title: Random allocation tests streptomycin for tuberculosis
milestones.summary: A Medical Research Council trial published in 1948 assigned patients with pulmonary tuberculosis to streptomycin or to usual care without it using random numbers held in sealed envelopes. It became a model for the randomised controlled trial.
milestones.explanation:
When the antibiotic streptomycin became available, the British Medical Research Council organised a trial in several hospitals. The statistician Austin Bradford Hill designed a scheme in which each patient's allocation was decided by random numbers, kept in sealed envelopes marked only with the hospital's name and a number, so that clinicians could not influence who received the drug.

The trial, reported in the British Medical Journal in 1948, found a markedly lower death rate among patients given streptomycin. Its lasting importance lay in its method: concealed random allocation protects comparisons from the conscious and unconscious choices of those running a trial.

Historians note that allocation by alternation had been used in earlier controlled trials, and that the word 'random' sometimes appeared in earlier reports when alternation was actually used.

milestones.title: Lithium tried for mania in Melbourne
milestones.summary: In 1949 the psychiatrist John Cade reported that lithium salts calmed patients with mania at a veterans' hospital in Melbourne, reviving a forgotten substance as a psychiatric treatment.
milestones.explanation:
John Cade was working at the Bundoora Repatriation Hospital, a veterans' hospital on the edge of Melbourne, when he began experiments based on a theory that mania might be caused by a toxic substance in the body. Giving lithium salts to laboratory animals, he noticed that they became calmer.

He then gave lithium citrate and lithium carbonate to ten patients with mania. Several improved strikingly, and he published the results in the Medical Journal of Australia in 1949. Lithium had been used in medicine in the nineteenth century, but its psychiatric use had been forgotten.

Cade's report was an uncontrolled case series. In Denmark, Mogens Schou tested lithium for mania in a trial that allocated patients to lithium or placebo, published in 1954. Uptake was uneven: the United States approved lithium only in 1970, becoming the 50th country to do so.

milestones.title: Polio vaccines tested on millions of children
milestones.summary: In 1954 about 1.8 million children in the United States, Canada and Finland took part in field trials of Jonas Salk's inactivated polio vaccine, announced as safe and effective on 12 April 1955. Albert Sabin's oral vaccine was then tested on a vast scale in the Soviet Union from 1958–59.
milestones.explanation:
Polio paralysed 13,000–20,000 people a year in the United States alone in the early 1950s. Salk, at the University of Pittsburgh, made a vaccine from killed poliovirus. The March of Dimes funded a field trial supervised by Thomas Francis Jr. of the University of Michigan: some children received vaccine or an injected placebo, with neither families nor officials knowing which, while others were observed as controls. On 12 April 1955 Francis announced that the vaccine was safe and effective, and it was licensed the same day.

Within weeks, two lots made by Cutter Laboratories turned out to contain live virus. Thousands of people received the faulty vaccine, and some developed paralysis.

Sabin's live, oral vaccine was tested instead, during the Cold War, in the Soviet Union, first on thousands and then on millions of children, before being adopted worldwide.

milestones.title: Aro village system: psychiatric care in the community
milestones.summary: From the mid-1950s, the Nigerian psychiatrist Thomas Adeoye Lambo, at the new Aro hospital in Abeokuta, arranged for patients to live in nearby villages during treatment, working with local communities and traditional healers.
milestones.explanation:
The Aro Mental Hospital opened in Abeokuta in 1954, under the British colonial government. Lambo, Nigeria's first Indigenous psychiatrist, had trained in Britain, including at the Maudsley Hospital, and returned in 1952. Rather than confining patients in wards, he arranged for them to live in surrounding villages while attending the hospital for treatment.

The Aro village system built on existing community structures, gave the villages health clinics and infrastructure in return, and drew traditional healers into care. It also supported research, such as the Cornell–Aro project, showing that major psychiatric disorders occurred in Nigeria in ways comparable to elsewhere.

The approach became an influential example of culturally grounded community psychiatry and inspired rehabilitation villages in Tanzania from 1969. Lambo later became Deputy Director-General of the World Health Organization.

milestones.title: The pressurised metered-dose asthma inhaler
milestones.summary: In 1956 Riker Laboratories in Los Angeles introduced the first pressurised metered-dose inhaler, prompted by a 13-year-old with asthma who asked why her medicine could not come in a spray can like hairspray.
milestones.explanation:
Before the inhaler, many people with asthma used fragile glass squeeze-bulb nebulisers. In 1955 Susie Maison asked her father George Maison, president of Riker Laboratories, a subsidiary of the Rexall drug company, whether her medicine could be delivered like aerosol hairspray. Riker's chemists Irving Porush and Charles Thiel, drawing on advice from Rexall's cosmetics laboratory, formulated asthma drugs with a propellant in a small pressurised canister with a valve that released a measured dose.

The device was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in March 1956 and marketed as the Medihaler. Pocket inhalers built on the same principle became the standard way of taking asthma medicines.

milestones.title: Ultrasound is used to look inside the abdomen and womb
milestones.summary: In June 1958 Ian Donald, John MacVicar and engineer Tom Brown in Glasgow reported using pulsed ultrasound to examine more than 100 patients, including pregnant women. Their team went on to build the first commercial ultrasound scanner, the Diasonograph, in 1963.
milestones.explanation:
Ian Donald, Regius Professor of Midwifery at the University of Glasgow, had seen industrial ultrasound flaw detectors used to find cracks in metal and wondered whether echoes could distinguish tissues in the body. Working with the obstetrician John MacVicar at the Western Infirmary and Tom Brown of the instrument makers Kelvin & Hughes, he built prototype scanners.

Their paper in The Lancet, 'Investigation of abdominal masses by pulsed ultrasound', showed images of ovarian cysts, fibroids and a fetal skull. The team's Diasonograph of 1963 was the first commercial ultrasound scanner, and ultrasound became a routine part of pregnancy care.

milestones.title: A pacemaker is implanted in a patient's body
milestones.summary: On 8 October 1958, at the Karolinska Hospital in Stockholm, the surgeon Åke Senning implanted a pacemaker built by the engineer Rune Elmqvist into Arne Larsson, a 43-year-old whose heart condition had become critical.
milestones.explanation:
Senning and Elmqvist, who worked for the company Elema-Schönander, were developing a fully implantable pacemaker but did not think it was ready for human use. Arne Larsson's heart condition had become life-threatening, and his wife Else-Marie, who had read about the experimental device in a newspaper, persuaded them to try it.

The first device was damaged during the operation and stopped working after the first night; an identical second device was implanted the next day, and Larsson's life was saved. Implantable pacemakers became a standard treatment for slow or blocked heart rhythms.

milestones.title: Chest compressions and rescue breathing become CPR
milestones.summary: In 1960 William Kouwenhoven, James Jude and Guy Knickerbocker at Johns Hopkins reported that pressing rhythmically on the chest could keep blood flowing during cardiac arrest. Combined with Peter Safar's mouth-to-mouth breathing, it became modern cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
milestones.explanation:
Kouwenhoven, an electrical engineer, was developing a closed-chest defibrillator at Johns Hopkins. During experiments on dogs, the team found that pressure on the sternum could keep enough blood circulating to the brain. With the surgeon James Jude they refined the technique and reported in 1960 that closed-chest cardiac massage had been used in 20 patients in hospital, 14 of whom survived.

Meanwhile Peter Safar and James Elam had shown in experiments on volunteers that mouth-to-mouth breathing ventilated the lungs better than the manual methods then in use. Safar, Kouwenhoven and Jude combined the two into CPR, which could be learned easily and done without equipment.

milestones.title: IVF works in a mammal: rabbits born from eggs fertilised in a dish
milestones.summary: In 1959 Min Chueh Chang at the Worcester Foundation in Massachusetts fertilised black rabbits' eggs with black rabbits' sperm in the laboratory and transferred them to a white female, which gave birth to black young. Chang, a reproductive biologist who had joined Gregory Pincus at the Worcester Foundation for Experimental Biology in 1945, designed an experiment whose result could not be mistaken: black offspring born to a white surrogate could only have come from black rabbits' eggs fertilised in the dish.

Chang went on to study in-vitro fertilisation in hamsters, mice and rats. His work helped form the basis for human IVF by Robert Edwards and Patrick Steptoe, which led to the birth of Louise Brown in 1978. He also contributed to the development of the contraceptive pill.

milestones.title: Benzodiazepines: Librium and Valium
milestones.summary: Leo Sternbach at Hoffmann-La Roche in Nutley, New Jersey, discovered the first benzodiazepine, chlordiazepoxide (Librium), marketed in 1960. Diazepam (Valium) followed in 1963 and became one of the most prescribed drugs in the world.
milestones.explanation:
In the 1950s anxiety and insomnia were treated mainly with barbiturates. Sternbach, a chemist at Roche's US research centre, had set aside a family of compounds when a colleague tidying the laboratory found one that had never been tested. Submitted in 1957, it proved a potent calming drug and was marketed as Librium in 1960.

Roche's chemists modified the molecule to produce diazepam, introduced in 1963 as Valium. Benzodiazepines at first appeared less toxic and less likely to cause dependence than older drugs, and Valium was the best-selling medicine in the United States from 1968 until 1982.

milestones.whatChanged: Anxiety, insomnia, muscle spasm and seizures could be treated with drugs that at first appeared much safer than barbiturates.
milestones.whyItMattered: Benzodiazepines are still used for anxiety and seizures, but their heavy use also showed how quickly a drug thought to be safe can create widespread dependence.
limitations: Benzodiazepines proved more habit-forming than first thought, and Valium's use declined in the 1980s because of its addictive properties.

milestones.title: A balloon catheter removes blood clots without opening the artery
milestones.summary: Thomas Fogarty, while a medical student in Cincinnati around 1960, devised a thin catheter with a small balloon at the tip that could be passed beyond a clot, inflated and pulled back to drag the clot out. Reported in 1963, it began catheter-based treatment of blood vessels.
milestones.explanation:
Fogarty, who had worked as a surgical scrub technician at Good Samaritan Hospital in Cincinnati, saw that the existing operations to remove clots from arteries often failed. As a medical student he designed a thin catheter with a balloon at its tip. Introduced through a small cut, the deflated balloon was pushed past the clot, inflated, and withdrawn, pulling the clot out.

With the vascular surgeon Jack Cranley, Fogarty first used it in a patient in the early 1960s and published the method in 1963. Surgeons were initially sceptical, because touching the inside of a vessel was thought to cause clotting.

date.basis: First use in a patient around 1961 according to the American College of Surgeons; publication and patent in 1963.

locations.name: University of Cincinnati and Good Samaritan Hospital, Cincinnati

people.name: Thomas Fogarty
people.role: Medical student and later surgeon; inventor

milestones.whatChanged: Clots could be removed from arteries through a small incision, saving limbs that might otherwise have been amputated.
milestones.whyItMattered: Balloon catheters became the basic tool of minimally invasive treatment inside blood vessels, leading to angioplasty and stents.
limitations: Balloons had been used on medical catheters before; the novelty was their use to extract clots.

milestones.title: Cochlear implants bring sound to deaf people
milestones.summary: William House and John Doyle implanted the first cochlear electrodes in Los Angeles in 1961. House's single-channel device, made with 3M, became in 1984 the first cochlear implant approved by the US FDA for adults.
milestones.explanation:
Cochlear implants stimulate the auditory nerve electrically, bypassing the damaged inner ear. After reading of earlier attempts in France, the otologist William House, with the neurosurgeon John Doyle and engineer James Doyle, implanted electrodes in three patients in 1961. Working with the engineer Jack Urban from the mid-1960s, House developed a wearable device with an induction coil that passed signals through the skin, used from 1972.

Many researchers doubted that a single electrode could be useful, but more than 1,000 adults received the House device, and a trial in the late 1970s found implants beneficial. Multichannel implants, developed by teams including Blair Simmons's in California and Claude-Henri Chouard's in Paris, later became the standard.

date.basis: First implants in 1961; wearable device from 1972; FDA approval in November 1984.

locations.name: Los Angeles Foundation of Otology (later House Ear Institute)

milestones.whatChanged: People with profound deafness could perceive sound through direct electrical stimulation of the auditory nerve.
milestones.whyItMattered: Cochlear implants have given many deaf children and adults access to sound and spoken language.
limitations: The single-channel House device mainly helped lip-reading; understanding speech without lip-reading came with multichannel implants.
French researchers had stimulated the auditory nerve in the late 1950s, so House was not the first to try.

milestones.title: Charnley's low-friction hip replacement
milestones.summary: In November 1962 John Charnley began using a hip replacement at Wrightington Hospital in Lancashire that combined a small polished metal ball with a high-density polyethylene socket, fixed with bone cement. It became the model for modern hip replacement.
milestones.explanation:
Earlier artificial hips often failed quickly. Charnley, an orthopaedic surgeon from Manchester, studied the friction of joint surfaces and moved his practice to a hip surgery centre at Wrightington Hospital in 1962. His first sockets of PTFE (Teflon) wore badly, so he switched to high-density polyethylene, which wore far more slowly.

He fixed the parts to bone with acrylic cement and used a clean-air enclosure in the operating theatre to reduce infection. Between November 1962 and 2005 more than 22,000 of his operations were performed at Wrightington alone.

date.basis: The Charnley low-friction arthroplasty was in use from November 1962, according to Wrightington's long-term follow-up.

milestones.whatChanged: A durable replacement for a painful arthritic hip became possible for large numbers of people.
milestones.whyItMattered: Hip replacement is now one of the most common and successful operations worldwide, relieving pain and restoring mobility.
limitations: Wear and loosening of the plastic socket remained the main long-term problems.
His first sockets, made of PTFE, failed and had to be abandoned.

milestones.title: Beta blockers: propranolol for heart disease
milestones.summary: At ICI's laboratories at Alderley Park, Cheshire, James Black and colleagues set out to block the effect of adrenaline on the heart. After an earlier compound, pronethalol, they developed propranolol, introduced in the mid-1960s and the first widely successful beta blocker.
milestones.explanation:
Black set out to protect the heart by blocking the beta receptors through which adrenaline acts on it, building on Raymond Ahlquist's work on adrenaline receptors. Joining ICI Pharmaceuticals in 1958, he worked with the chemist John Stephenson and others. They derived propranolol from earlier compounds, dichloroisoprenaline and pronethalol; it was patented in 1962.

Propranolol revolutionised the treatment of ischaemic heart disease and was later used widely for high blood pressure. Black went on to develop cimetidine for stomach ulcers, and shared the 1988 Nobel Prize for his approach to designing drugs.

date.basis: Pronethalol introduced and propranolol patented in 1962; propranolol approved for medical use around 1964–65.

people.name: Brian Pritchard
people.role: Clinical pharmacologist who led clinical development

milestones.whatChanged: Doctors could reduce the heart's workload by blocking adrenaline's effects, treating angina and later high blood pressure.
milestones.whyItMattered: Beta blockers became among the most widely used heart drugs, and Black's receptor-targeted approach became a model for drug discovery.
limitations: Sources differ on whether propranolol's approval should be dated 1964 or 1965.
An earlier beta blocker, pronethalol, preceded propranolol; 'first' here means the first widely successful one.

milestones.title: The first human lung transplant, in Jackson, Mississippi
milestones.summary: On 11 June 1963 James Hardy's team at the University of Mississippi Medical Center transplanted a lung into John Russell, a 58-year-old prisoner with lung cancer. Russell lived 18 days and died of kidney failure.
milestones.explanation:
James Hardy's medical school dean granted him permission to attempt a human lung transplant under agreed conditions. John Russell, serving a life sentence at the Mississippi State Penitentiary, had a tumour blocking his left main airway and emphysema in his right lung. He received the left lung of a patient who had died of a heart attack.

The new lung worked, but Russell died 18 days later of kidney failure. The first lung transplant with long-term success came only in 1983.

date.basis: Operation performed on the night of 11–12 June 1963.

locations.name: University Hospital, University of Mississippi Medical Center, Jackson

milestones.whatChanged: It showed that a human lung could be transplanted and function in a recipient.
milestones.whyItMattered: It opened clinical lung transplantation, now a treatment for end-stage lung disease, though decades passed before it succeeded routinely.
limitations: It was the first lung transplant in a human, not the first lasting success: long-term success came only in 1983.
The patient survived only 18 days.
milestones.harms: The recipient was a prisoner serving a life sentence. Historians have noted the ethical questions raised by recruiting prisoners for first-in-human operations, a common practice in the US at the time.

milestones.title: A measles vaccine is licensed
milestones.summary: John Enders and Thomas Peebles isolated measles virus in Boston in 1954 from a schoolboy, David Edmonston. Enders' team weakened it into a vaccine that was licensed in the United States in 1963; an improved version from 1968 is still used.
milestones.explanation:
Before the vaccine, nearly every American child caught measles by the age of 15, and it still killed about 500 Americans a year. During an outbreak at a boarding school near Boston in 1954, Peebles, a young paediatrician working with Enders at Boston Children's Hospital, collected samples; the virus from David Edmonston was grown in cell culture and gradually weakened.

The Edmonston-B vaccine was tested in small groups of children from 1958 and then in larger trials in New York and Nigeria. It was licensed in March 1963, but often caused fever and rash; Maurice Hilleman of Merck produced a further-weakened version in 1968, the only measles vaccine used in the United States since.

milestones.whatChanged: Measles, previously almost universal in childhood, could be prevented.
milestones.whyItMattered: Widespread measles vaccination drastically reduced one of the most contagious childhood diseases.
limitations: The first vaccine frequently caused fever and rash and was soon superseded.
Sources disagree on David Edmonston's age at the time (11 or 13).

milestones.title: Liver transplantation: first attempts and first success
milestones.summary: Thomas Starzl attempted the first human liver transplants in Denver in 1963, but the early operations did not succeed. In 1967 he achieved the first successful liver transplant, at the University of Colorado.
milestones.explanation:
The liver's complexity and the strength of rejection made it far harder to transplant than the kidney. Starzl, who had built an active kidney transplant programme at the University of Colorado and the Denver Veterans Administration Hospital, performed the first human liver transplants in 1963, using azathioprine and steroids to control rejection.

In 1967 Starzl's team carried out the first successful liver transplant. He later helped bring the immunosuppressants cyclosporine and tacrolimus into transplant practice, which made liver transplants far more reliable.

date.basis: First attempts in 1963; first successful transplant in 1967.

locations.name: University of Colorado and Denver Veterans Administration Hospital

milestones.whatChanged: Replacing a failed liver became possible, offering survival to people with otherwise fatal liver disease.
milestones.whyItMattered: Liver transplantation is now a standard treatment for end-stage liver disease and some liver cancers.
limitations: The 1963 operations did not achieve lasting success.
Sources give different dates in 1963 for the first operations.

sources.supports: Joined the University of Colorado in 1962; kidney transplants from 1962; liver transplantation from 1963 and first successful liver transplant in 1967 at the University of Colorado and Denver VA Hospitals; steroids added to azathioprine; later cyclosporine and tacrolimus.

milestones.title: A portable defibrillator takes heart-attack care to the patient
milestones.summary: In 1966 Frank Pantridge and John Geddes of the Royal Victoria Hospital, Belfast, launched a mobile coronary care unit: an ambulance carrying a doctor and a portable defibrillator to treat cardiac arrest before patients reached hospital.
milestones.explanation:
Pantridge had opened a coronary care unit in Belfast in late 1963, but argued that such units would be of little value if patients died before reaching hospital. With Geddes and the engineer John Anderson, he built a defibrillator that could run from a car battery; the first version, in 1965, weighed about 70 kg.

From 1966 a team travelled from the Royal Victoria Hospital to patients at the request of their family doctors. A 1967 editorial in The Lancet said that Pantridge and Geddes had revolutionised emergency medicine, and by 1968 Pantridge had a version weighing 3 kg. The 'Pantridge plan' was copied in many countries and led to the automated external defibrillator.

date.basis: First portable defibrillator in 1965; mobile coronary care unit from 1966; Lancet report in 1967.

milestones.whatChanged: Cardiac arrest could be treated at the scene, in the minutes when defibrillation is most effective.
milestones.whyItMattered: Pre-hospital cardiac care and paramedic defibrillation spread worldwide, and the portable defibrillator evolved into the public-access AEDs found in public places today.
limitations: The first portable unit was heavy and needed its own vehicle.
Similar mobile units were soon set up elsewhere, including New York in 1967.

milestones.title: The first pancreas transplant, in Minneapolis
milestones.summary: On 16–17 December 1966 William Kelly and Richard Lillehei at the University of Minnesota transplanted a pancreas together with a kidney into a 28-year-old woman with diabetic kidney failure. It showed for the first time that a transplanted pancreas could free a person with type 1 diabetes from insulin.
milestones.explanation:
People with type 1 diabetes depend on injected insulin and often develop kidney failure. Kelly and Lillehei transplanted part of a pancreas and a kidney from a deceased donor into a 28-year-old woman with kidney failure; for the first time, a person with type 1 diabetes became independent of insulin.

The University of Minnesota went on to perform more than 1,000 pancreas transplants, and outcomes improved with better immunosuppression. More than 50,000 pancreas transplants have since been performed worldwide.

milestones.whatChanged: It showed that transplanting a pancreas could restore the body's own insulin production.
milestones.whyItMattered: Pancreas transplantation, usually with a kidney, became a treatment for people with type 1 diabetes and kidney failure.
limitations: The earliest pancreas transplants had a high failure rate.
Sources differ on whether the operation took place on 16 or 17 December 1966.

milestones.title: Coronary bypass surgery with a leg vein
milestones.summary: On 9 May 1967 the Argentine surgeon René Favaloro, working at the Cleveland Clinic, used a segment of the patient's saphenous vein to carry blood past a blocked coronary artery. Coronary artery bypass grafting became one of the most common heart operations.
milestones.explanation:
Favaloro had studied thousands of the coronary angiograms made by Mason Sones at the Cleveland Clinic, which showed exactly where arteries were blocked. Earlier surgeons had experimented with other approaches, and Vasilii Kolesov in Leningrad had performed internal thoracic artery bypasses from 1964. Favaloro's systematic use of vein grafts from the leg, guided by angiography, made the operation reproducible.

He performed 13 more operations by October 1967 and published his results in 1968; by 1970 he and his colleagues had carried out more than 1,000.

date.basis: Date of Favaloro's first saphenous vein bypass; results published in April 1968.

milestones.whatChanged: Blocked coronary arteries could be bypassed, relieving angina and restoring blood flow to the heart muscle.
milestones.whyItMattered: Bypass surgery became a mainstay of treatment for coronary heart disease worldwide.
limitations: Priority is debated: Kolesov in Leningrad, Robert Goetz and others performed earlier coronary bypass operations.
At first surgeons disagreed about which patients benefited, and long-term results were studied for years afterwards.

milestones.title: The first human heart transplant, Cape Town
milestones.summary: In the early hours of 3 December 1967, at Groote Schuur Hospital, a team led by Christiaan Barnard transplanted the heart of Denise Darvall, a 25-year-old killed in a road accident, into Louis Washkansky. He lived for 18 days.
milestones.explanation:
Barnard had established an open-heart surgery programme at Groote Schuur Hospital and the University of Cape Town in 1958. Several teams in the United States had prepared for heart transplantation through years of animal research and were close to attempting it.

Denise Darvall was struck by a car outside a bakery in Observatory, Cape Town, and declared brain dead. Her heart was transplanted into Louis Washkansky, a 54-year-old with severe heart failure, and was shocked into beating just before 6 a.m. on 3 December. He died 18 days later of pneumonia. Barnard's second patient, Philip Blaiberg, lived for about 19 months.

The operation drew worldwide attention, and surgeons elsewhere, including Euryclides Zerbini's team in Brazil, began preparing their own transplants within days.

Early survival was short: Washkansky died of pneumonia, and rejection was not recognised in time.

milestones.title: Mumps vaccine, then the combined MMR vaccine
milestones.summary: Maurice Hilleman of Merck isolated mumps virus from his daughter Jeryl Lynn in 1963 and developed a vaccine licensed in 1967. In 1971 he combined it with measles and rubella vaccines into MMR.
milestones.explanation:
When his five-year-old daughter Jeryl Lynn fell ill with mumps in March 1963, Hilleman, head of virus research at the Merck Institute in West Point, Pennsylvania, swabbed her throat and grew the virus in the laboratory. Weakened by passage through chick embryo cells, the 'Jeryl Lynn' strain became the mumps vaccine licensed in 1967 and is still used.

In 1971 Merck's combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine was licensed in the United States, allowing children to be protected against three diseases with fewer injections.

milestones.title: Smallpox eradicated
milestones.summary: After an intensified WHO-led campaign launched in 1967, the last natural case of smallpox occurred in Merca, Somalia, in October 1977. In May 1980 the World Health Assembly declared the disease eradicated.
milestones.explanation:
Smallpox had afflicted humanity for at least 3,000 years and, by WHO's estimate, killed some 300 million people in the twentieth century alone. In 1967 the World Health Organization launched an intensified eradication programme, which worked by identifying every case and its contacts and making sure they were vaccinated. Within four years the disease was gone from Latin America; four more years ended it in Asia.

The final naturally acquired case was Ali Maow Maalin, a 23-year-old hospital cook and former vaccinator in Merca, Somalia, who fell ill after guiding a vehicle carrying two infected children in October 1977. He recovered and later worked in Somalia's polio eradication campaign.

After two years of searching for any remaining transmission, an independent Global Commission certified eradication in December 1979, and on 8 May 1980 the World Health Assembly formally declared it. A laboratory accident in Birmingham, England, in 1978 caused the last known cases and one death.

milestones.title: Oral rehydration: sugar and salt water against cholera
milestones.summary: Trials in Dhaka in 1968 showed that a solution of glucose and salt taken by mouth could replace much of the intravenous fluid needed in cholera. In 1971, in refugee camps during the Bangladesh Liberation War, Dilip Mahalanabis showed it worked even where families gave it themselves.
milestones.explanation:
Untreated cholera killed 30–40 per cent of patients, and intravenous fluids, the only effective treatment, were difficult and costly to provide in large outbreaks. Researchers in Dhaka (then East Pakistan) and Calcutta found that the intestine continues to absorb salt and water in cholera if glucose is present.

At the Cholera Research Laboratory in Dhaka, Richard Cash and David Nalin successfully tested an oral glucose–salt solution in 29 patients, publishing in The Lancet in 1968. In 1971, as refugees fled to India during the war that created Bangladesh, cholera broke out in the camps. Mahalanabis, of the Johns Hopkins centre in Calcutta, used drums of oral solution administered largely by family members, and the case fatality rate fell significantly.

In 1978 The Lancet called the discovery potentially the most important medical advance of the century. Even so, persuading sceptical clinicians that minimally trained people could give it took years.

milestones.title: Controlled-release drugs and the first skin patch
milestones.summary: Alejandro Zaffaroni founded ALZA in Palo Alto in 1968 to release drugs at a steady, controlled rate. After an eye insert for glaucoma in 1974, ALZA's scopolamine patch for motion sickness became in 1981 the first transdermal drug patch approved in the United States.
milestones.explanation:
Pills and injections deliver drugs in peaks and troughs. Its first approved product, in 1974, was Ocusert, a thin film placed in the eye that released the glaucoma drug pilocarpine.

Working with Ciba-Geigy, ALZA gained approval for Transderm Scop in August 1981, followed two months later by a nitroglycerin patch for angina. Patches for nicotine and pain relief followed.

milestones.title: Rubella vaccines protect unborn babies
milestones.summary: After a rubella epidemic in 1964–65 left thousands of American babies with birth defects, vaccines were developed by Harry Meyer and Paul Parkman at the US National Institutes of Health and by Stanley Plotkin at the Wistar Institute. The first were licensed in 1969.
milestones.explanation:

Parkman, who had helped isolate the virus at the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research, and Meyer at the NIH's Division of Biologics Standards weakened a strain, HPV-77, which was among three vaccines licensed in the United States in 1969. At the Wistar Institute in Philadelphia, Plotkin developed the RA 27/3 strain in human cells; licensed in the UK in 1972 and in the US in 1979, it is the basis of most rubella vaccines, including MMR, today.

milestones.title: The first CT scan of a patient's brain
milestones.summary: On 1 October 1971 at Atkinson Morley's Hospital in London, a prototype scanner built by the EMI engineer Godfrey Hounsfield produced a cross-sectional X-ray image of a living patient's brain, revealing a tumour.
milestones.explanation:
Conventional X-rays superimpose everything in their path onto a single picture. Hounsfield, an engineer at EMI, conceived of taking many X-ray measurements from different angles and using a computer to reconstruct a slice through the body. EMI, flush with income from its music business, and the British Department of Health funded the work.

The prototype was installed at Atkinson Morley's Hospital, where the radiologist James Ambrose scanned the first patient on 1 October 1971: the image showed a cystic tumour in the frontal lobe, and the surgeon later confirmed it looked as the picture predicted. Each slice took minutes to acquire and longer to compute, but neurologists around the world quickly sought the new machines.

The physicist Allan Cormack had independently worked out the mathematics of reconstructing images from projections. He and Hounsfield shared the 1979 Nobel Prize.

milestones.title: Artemisinin extracted from qinghao
milestones.summary: Working within China's secret national malaria programme, Project 523, Tu Youyou's group found that a low-temperature extract of qinghao (Artemisia annua) cleared malaria parasites in animals in 1971 and in patients in 1972.
milestones.explanation:
In the 1960s Chinese military institutes began confidential research on drugs against malaria, and in 1967 a national office was set up to coordinate the work, known as Project 523. In 1969 Tu Youyou, at the Institute of Chinese Materia Medica in Beijing, was appointed to lead a group searching traditional Chinese medicine for candidates.

Early extracts of qinghao gave inconsistent results. A passage in Ge Hong's Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies describes soaking the herb in cold water and wringing out the juice, rather than boiling it. Suspecting that heat destroyed the active ingredient, Tu's group changed to low-temperature extraction. On 4 October 1971, sample 191, an ether extract, completely inhibited malaria parasites in rodents.

Between August and October 1972 the extract was tested on 21 patients in Hainan, all of whom lost their fever and parasites, and on further patients in Beijing. Other institutions helped determine the structure of the active compound, artemisinin. Artemisinin-based combination therapies later became the standard treatment for falciparum malaria worldwide.

milestones.title: Auckland trial shows steroids before birth protect premature babies
milestones.summary: In 1972 Graham Liggins and Ross Howie published the first randomised, placebo-controlled trial of giving corticosteroids to mothers at risk of preterm birth. Babies whose mothers received betamethasone had less respiratory distress and lower mortality.
milestones.explanation:
The idea came from sheep. Liggins, an obstetrician in Auckland, was infusing pregnant ewes with corticosteroids to study what triggers labour. One delivered a lamb so premature it should not have survived, yet it was breathing. Its lungs had matured faster than expected.

With the paediatrician Ross Howie, Liggins designed a double-blind trial at a tertiary obstetric hospital in Auckland: women at risk of preterm birth received betamethasone or a matching placebo. The steroid reduced neonatal respiratory distress syndrome and deaths, and appeared safe in the short term. Follow-up of the trial's children has continued for decades, into adulthood.

Antenatal corticosteroids became a cornerstone of care for threatened preterm birth worldwide, although adoption was slow for years after the trial, and questions about timing and dose are still being studied.

milestones.title: Alma-Ata declares primary health care the route to 'Health for All'
milestones.summary: On 12 September 1978, the International Conference on Primary Health Care in Alma-Ata, in the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic, adopted a declaration calling health a fundamental human right and primary health care the key to health for all.
milestones.explanation:
The conference, convened by WHO and UNICEF, brought together delegations from 134 countries. Its declaration defined health broadly, as complete physical, mental and social well-being, and called existing inequalities in health between and within countries politically, socially and economically unacceptable.

It set the goal of 'Health for All by the Year 2000' and argued that this could be reached through primary health care: essential, accessible care close to where people live and work, with community participation and action across sectors beyond health.

The goal was not met, and in the following years many programmes narrowed to selected interventions. But primary health care became a core concept for WHO, and in 2018 the Declaration of Astana, in the same country, reaffirmed Alma-Ata as the foundation for universal health coverage.

milestones.whyItMattered: Shaped four decades of health-system planning and remains the reference point for universal health coverage.
limitations: A declaration is a commitment, not an outcome; 'Health for All by 2000' was not achieved.
Its broad vision was soon narrowed in practice to selected, targeted programmes in many countries.

milestones.title: Two IVF births in 1978: Oldham and Calcutta
milestones.summary: On 25 July 1978 Louise Brown was born in Oldham, England, after in vitro fertilisation by Robert Edwards, Patrick Steptoe and Jean Purdy. Sixty-seven days later, on 3 October, a team in Calcutta led by Subhas Mukhopadhyay announced the birth of Durga (Kanupriya Agarwal).
milestones.explanation:
Robert Edwards had pursued the idea of fertilising human eggs outside the body since the 1950s. With the gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe, who retrieved eggs by laparoscopy, and the embryologist and nurse Jean Purdy, he worked through years of experiments and failures. Louise Brown, born at Oldham General Hospital, was the first child conceived through IVF.

In Calcutta, Subhas Mukhopadhyay, with Sunit Mukherjee and the gynaecologist Saroj Kanti Bhattacharya, used a different approach, including ovarian stimulation, and announced the birth of Durga on 3 October 1978. Both announcements met scepticism. The British team went on to further births; Mukhopadhyay was transferred to an eye hospital and could not continue his work. Today his team's work is widely acknowledged as the world's second IVF birth.

IVF has since led to millions of births worldwide. Edwards received the Nobel Prize in 2010.

milestones.title: Kangaroo mother care begins in Bogotá
milestones.summary: In 1978, faced with overcrowding and too few incubators, neonatologists Edgar Rey Sanabria and Héctor Martínez at Bogotá's Instituto Materno Infantil began keeping small and premature babies in continuous skin-to-skin contact with their mothers.
milestones.explanation:
The method has three parts: the baby is held upright against the mother's (or another carer's) bare chest, is breastfed, ideally exclusively, and goes home early with close follow-up. It was devised as an alternative to scarce and sometimes unsafe incubator care.

The idea spread from Colombia to Brazil and well beyond. Randomised trials followed: a Cochrane review of 21 studies including more than 3,000 low-birthweight infants found better growth with kangaroo care, and later reviews report lower mortality compared with standard care, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. WHO now recommends it for clinically stable newborns weighing 2,000 g or less.

Kangaroo care shows a pattern common in medicine: a practical solution from a resource-constrained setting, later confirmed by trials and adopted in wealthy countries too.

milestones.title: Stomach ulcers traced to a bacterium
milestones.summary: In Perth, the pathologist Robin Warren and the physician Barry Marshall showed that curved bacteria, later named Helicobacter pylori, live in the stomach and cause gastritis and most peptic ulcers.
milestones.explanation:
Robin Warren noticed small curved bacteria on stomach biopsies, in the lower part of the stomach of about half of patients examined, always alongside inflammation. Together with Barry Marshall, he set out to test the link. After several failed attempts, Marshall succeeded in growing the bacterium in culture in 1982.

At the time, stress and lifestyle were considered the main causes of peptic ulcer, and the idea that bacteria could survive in the acid stomach met resistance. Marshall and Warren went on to show that the bacterium causes gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.

Peptic ulcer disease, often chronic and recurrent, became curable with a short course of antibiotics and acid-reducing drugs.

date.basis: Year in which the bacterium was cultured and the discovery made, as dated by the Nobel Assembly.

people.name: J. Robin Warren
people.role: Pathologist; first linked the bacteria to inflammation

people.role: Physician; cultured the bacterium and showed its role in ulcers

milestones.whatChanged: Reclassified most peptic ulcers as an infectious disease that antibiotics can cure.
milestones.whyItMattered: Turned a chronic, recurring condition into a curable one, and showed how an established consensus can be overturned by evidence.
limitations: Not all ulcers are caused by H. pylori; anti-inflammatory drugs are another major cause.
Most people infected with H. pylori never develop an ulcer.

sources.supports: Warren, a pathologist from Perth, saw curved bacteria in about 50% of biopsies; discovery dated 1982; Marshall cultivated the bacterium; stress and lifestyle previously considered the major causes; cure with antibiotics and acid secretion inhibitors.

milestones.title: The virus that causes AIDS is isolated
milestones.summary: In 1983 Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, Luc Montagnier and colleagues at the Institut Pasteur isolated a new retrovirus from the lymph node of a patient at risk of AIDS. It became known as HIV.
milestones.explanation:
By the early 1980s many researchers suspected that AIDS had an infectious cause, and the Paris team decided to test whether it might be a retrovirus. The Paris team cultured lymph node cells from patients with swollen lymph glands and early signs of immune damage, and detected a new retrovirus, which they called lymphadenopathy-associated virus (LAV), publishing in Science in 1983.

In 1984, Robert Gallo's group at the US National Institutes of Health reported a virus from many patients, named HTLV-III, and Jay Levy's group in San Francisco separately identified a related virus. The viruses proved to be the same, and in 1985 an international committee named it human immunodeficiency virus.

Identifying the virus led to blood tests that protected blood supplies and allowed diagnosis, and to antiretroviral drugs. Combination therapy greatly extended life expectancy where it was available; the drugs suppress the virus but do not cure the infection.

milestones.whyItMattered: Underpins every later advance in HIV prevention and treatment.
limitations: Access to antiretroviral treatment has been, and remains, unequal across the world.
Treatment controls HIV but does not cure it.

milestones.title: A portable pressure bag for altitude sickness
milestones.summary: Igor Gamow of the University of Colorado, Boulder, patented a lightweight, inflatable hyperbaric chamber in 1990. Pumped up around a climber, it simulates a lower altitude and is used to treat severe mountain sickness where descent is not possible.
milestones.explanation:
Severe altitude illness, including fluid on the lungs or brain, is treated by descending. When that is impossible, raising the air pressure around the patient has a similar effect. Gamow and Geoffrey Geer first patented a portable chamber for studying exercise at raised pressure; the design they patented in the United States in 1990 was a backpackable, inflatable bag about the size of a sleeping bag.

Portable hyperbaric bags are now recommended for severe mountain sickness when descent is risky. A case report from Mount Everest describes a climber with high-altitude pulmonary oedema treated in a Gamow bag for two hours at 7,060 m before descending safely.

date.basis: US patent 4,974,829 granted on 4 December 1990; related European filings date from 1988–89.

milestones.whatChanged: Climbers with severe altitude illness could be treated on the mountain when bad weather, darkness or injury prevented descent.
milestones.whyItMattered: It gave expedition doctors a way to buy time in an emergency at altitude.
limitations: The bag is a temporary measure: descent remains the definitive treatment.
Evidence for its benefit comes mainly from case reports and small studies.

milestones.title: Vaccines against hepatitis A are licensed
milestones.summary: An inactivated hepatitis A vaccine, Havrix, was licensed in Europe in 1991 after development involving GSK Biologicals in Belgium and US government laboratories. A live attenuated vaccine was licensed in China in 1992.
milestones.explanation:
Hepatitis A virus was identified by electron microscopy at the US National Institutes of Health, but a vaccine depended on growing it in cell cultures suitable for manufacture. Havrix, a formalin-inactivated vaccine, built on strain HM-175 and work in Robert Purcell's laboratory at the NIH, with human trials at the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research from 1986 and a phase 3 trial in Thailand. It was developed by SmithKline Beecham Biologicals at Rixensart, Belgium, licensed in Europe in 1991 and in the United States in 1995.

China took a different route: a live attenuated vaccine based on the H2 strain was licensed there in 1992. Vaccination of children in several countries has since been followed by large falls in hepatitis A.

milestones.whyItMattered: Vaccination has been followed by steep declines in hepatitis A in countries including the United States, Israel and Argentina.

More than 7,000 people still died of hepatitis A worldwide in 2016.

milestones.title: Injecting a single sperm into an egg: ICSI in Brussels
milestones.summary: In 1992 a team at the Free University of Brussels reported pregnancies and births after injecting a single sperm directly into a human egg. Intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) became the standard treatment for severe male infertility.
milestones.explanation:
In-vitro fertilisation often failed when sperm were few or poorly motile. The Brussels Centre for Reproductive Medicine, headed by André Van Steirteghem and Paul Devroey, had been placing sperm under the egg's outer coat (subzonal insemination). The team, including Gianpiero Palermo, also began injecting a sperm directly into some eggs, and found fertilisation much more consistent that way; a pregnancy from such an embryo in April 1991 led to a birth on 14 January 1992.

They abandoned the older method and reported in The Lancet in July 1992: of 47 eggs injected, 31 fertilised, and four pregnancies resulted, with four healthy babies delivered.

milestones.whyItMattered: ICSI made severe male-factor infertility treatable and is now one of the most widely used procedures in assisted reproduction.
limitations: Earlier attempts at microinjection had been made elsewhere with little success.
Follow-up studies monitor genetic and developmental outcomes, since some causes of male infertility can be passed on.

milestones.title: A vaccine against the virus behind cervical cancer
milestones.summary: Ian Frazer and Jian Zhou at the University of Queensland made virus-like particles that mimic human papillomavirus (HPV) from 1991. The technology led to Gardasil, approved in Australia and the United States in 2006 to prevent infection with the HPV types that cause most cervical cancers.
milestones.explanation:
Certain HPV types cause cervical cancer; types 16 and 18 alone cause about 70% of cases. The live virus could not be grown in the laboratory to make a conventional vaccine. Frazer, an immunologist in Brisbane, met the virologist Jian Zhou in Cambridge in 1989 and invited him to Queensland. With Xiao-Yi Sun and others they produced HPV surface proteins that self-assembled into empty, non-infectious shells resembling the virus, which provoke a strong antibody response.

In 1995 the technology was licensed through CSL to Merck, whose vaccine Gardasil, covering HPV types 6, 11, 16 and 18, was approved in 2006; GSK's Cervarix, also based on virus-like particles, followed. Zhou died in 1999, before the vaccine reached use.

milestones.whatChanged: Infection with the main cancer-causing HPV types could be prevented, rather than its consequences only detected by screening.
milestones.whyItMattered: Vaccination programmes are expected to prevent most cervical cancers and some other HPV-related cancers.
limitations: The vaccines are given before exposure, typically to adolescents; they prevent new infections rather than treating existing ones.
Most deaths from cervical cancer occur in low-income countries; the University of Queensland waived royalties in 72 developing countries to widen access.

milestones.title: Brugada syndrome described as a cause of sudden cardiac death
milestones.summary: In 1992 Pedro and Josep Brugada described eight people who had survived sudden cardiac arrest despite structurally normal hearts, all sharing a distinctive ECG pattern. The condition, now called Brugada syndrome, is an inherited cause of sudden death.
milestones.explanation:
The Brugadas' multicentre report in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology described six men and two women with repeated episodes of aborted sudden death that no known disease explained. During normal rhythm their ECGs showed a right bundle branch block pattern with persistent ST-segment elevation in the right chest leads; the fatal rhythm was a rapid polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.

Naming the pattern made it possible to recognise people at risk from a routine ECG. Later research linked the syndrome to inherited faults in the genes for heart ion channels, and drugs such as ajmaline or flecainide came to be used to unmask concealed forms.

date.basis: Publication date of the report in J Am Coll Cardiol 20(6).

milestones.locationNote: A multicentre report; the sources checked do not tie the description to one place.
milestones.whatChanged: A specific ECG pattern could be linked to a high risk of sudden death in people with otherwise normal hearts.
milestones.whyItMattered: It explains some sudden deaths in young adults and children, and allows relatives and at-risk people to be screened and protected, for example with an implanted defibrillator.
limitations: Many people with the ECG pattern but no symptoms are at low risk, so deciding whom to treat remains difficult.
milestones.contested: Martini and colleagues had described patients with a similar ECG pattern and ventricular fibrillation in 1989, though they reported subtle structural abnormalities of the right ventricle.

milestones.title: Dolly the sheep is cloned from an adult cell
milestones.summary: Dolly, born at the Roslin Institute near Edinburgh on 5 July 1996, was the first mammal cloned from a fully specialised adult cell. Her birth showed that an adult cell's DNA could still direct the development of a whole animal.
milestones.explanation:
Earlier experiments had cloned amphibians, and the Roslin team had cloned the sheep Megan and Morag from cultured embryo cells in 1995. Many believed that fully specialised adult cells could not be reprogrammed in this way. Ian Wilmut, Keith Campbell and colleagues used somatic cell nuclear transfer, placing the nucleus of an udder cell from a six-year-old Finn Dorset ewe into an egg cell, and transferred the resulting embryo to a surrogate.

Dolly's birth was announced in February 1997 with the publication of 'Viable offspring derived from fetal and adult mammalian cells' in Nature. The experiment is widely seen as a stepping stone from earlier amphibian cloning to the reprogramming of adult human cells into stem cells.

date.basis: Date of Dolly's birth; the result was published on 27 February 1997.

milestones.whatChanged: It showed that the genetic material of specialised adult cells can be reprogrammed to produce a complete animal.
milestones.whyItMattered: It overturned a central assumption of developmental biology and opened the path to reprogramming adult cells for regenerative medicine, while prompting wide ethical debate about cloning.
limitations: Dolly was one success among many failed attempts, and cloning remains inefficient.
Dolly was not the first cloned mammal: sheep had been cloned from embryo cells before.

milestones.title: Human embryonic stem cells are grown in the laboratory
milestones.summary: In November 1998 James Thomson's team at the University of Wisconsin–Madison reported five lines of human embryonic stem cells, derived from donated IVF embryos. The cells could multiply indefinitely and form tissues of all three germ layers.
milestones.explanation:
James Thomson, chief pathologist at the Wisconsin Regional Primate Research Center, began work on embryonic stem cells in 1995. His team took the inner cell mass from human blastocysts, embryos a few days old donated by couples who had undergone IVF, and established five cell lines with normal chromosomes and high telomerase activity. The cells could form tissues of all three germ layers, including gut lining, cartilage, bone, muscle and nerve tissue.

A team led by John Gearhart published a related method from germ cells shortly afterwards. Human embryonic stem cells became a major tool for studying development and testing drugs, and the basis for experimental cell therapies.

date.basis: Publication date in Science 282:1145–1147.

milestones.whatChanged: Human cells able to become any tissue could be grown and studied in quantity.
milestones.whyItMattered: It opened research into human development, disease modelling and cell replacement, and led to sustained public debate over the use of human embryos.
limitations: Deriving the cells destroys the embryo, which has made the research ethically and politically contested.
Treatments based on the cells have been slow to reach patients.
