milestones.title: Ghrelin, a hunger hormone from the stomach, is identified
milestones.summary: In 1999 Masayasu Kojima, Kenji Kangawa and colleagues in Osaka identified ghrelin, a 28-amino-acid peptide made in the stomach. It releases growth hormone and turned out to stimulate appetite.
milestones.explanation:
Synthetic drugs had been found to release growth hormone through a receptor whose natural signal was unknown. Kangawa's group at the National Cardiovascular Center Research Institute in Suita, Osaka, purified the missing natural signal from rat stomach. It was a peptide of 28 amino acids with an unusual fatty-acid modification, and they named it ghrelin.

Later work showed that ghrelin also stimulates appetite, earning it the nickname 'hunger hormone'. It has since been studied in obesity, wasting and heart failure.

milestones.whyItMattered: It changed understanding of how appetite and energy balance are regulated and opened new lines of research on obesity and wasting.
limitations: The original discovery was made in rats; the hormone's role in human appetite was established by later studies.
Drugs targeting ghrelin have had limited clinical success so far.

milestones.title: A swallowable camera pill images the small bowel
milestones.summary: In 2000 Gavriel Iddan of Given Imaging in Israel and Paul Swain of the Royal London Hospital described a wireless capsule endoscope: a pill containing a camera, light and transmitter that photographs the gut as it passes through.
milestones.explanation:
Most of the small intestine was hard to reach with conventional endoscopes. Iddan, an electro-optical engineer, began working on a swallowable camera in Israel in the early 1990s, while Swain pursued similar ideas in London; the two groups joined forces from 1998, and Given Imaging was founded in Yokneam to develop the device. Swain was the first person to swallow it, in October 1999.

The team reported the device in Nature in May 2000, and in January 2001 published the first images of disease in the human small bowel taken with it, in patients with unexplained bleeding.

milestones.whatChanged: The whole small intestine could be examined without sedation or a flexible tube.
milestones.whyItMattered: It became a standard way to look for hidden bleeding and other disease in the small bowel.
limitations: The capsule cannot take biopsies or treat what it finds.
Swain and Iddan had worked on the idea separately for years before combining efforts, so credit is shared.

milestones.title: The Human Genome Project publishes a draft, then a near-complete sequence
milestones.summary: An international consortium of 20 groups in six countries published a draft human genome sequence in 2001 and announced an essentially complete sequence in April 2003, two years ahead of schedule. It covered about 92% of the genome.
milestones.explanation:
The Human Genome Project began formally in 1990, when the US National Institutes of Health and Department of Energy published a plan for the first five years of an expected 15-year effort. Sequencing was carried out by the International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium: 20 groups in the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan, France, Germany and China. A draft was announced in June 2000 and published in Nature in February 2001, alongside a competing draft from the company Celera Genomics.

In April 2003 the consortium announced an essentially complete sequence, as complete as the sequencing technology of the time allowed. The project also changed scientific practice: the sequence was released publicly shortly after it was produced, under the 1996 Bermuda Principles on open data.

date.basis: Draft announced in June 2000 and published on 15 February 2001; completion announced in April 2003. The project itself began in 1990.

milestones.title: Surgeons in New York operate on a patient in Strasbourg
milestones.summary: On 7 September 2001 Jacques Marescaux's team in New York removed the gallbladder of a patient in Strasbourg using a surgical robot controlled over a transatlantic high-speed link. The 'Lindbergh operation' showed that long-distance surgery was technically feasible.
milestones.explanation:
Keyhole surgery already put a screen between surgeon and patient. The question was whether that distance could be thousands of kilometres without a dangerous delay between the surgeon's movement and the robot's response. Marescaux's institute in Strasbourg, IRCAD, founded in 1994 to link surgery and computing, set out to reduce that delay using the Zeus surgical robot and a high-speed telecommunications link.

The patient, fully informed, was operated on under general anaesthesia at Strasbourg's university hospital while the surgeons worked in New York. The operation was reported in Nature that month.

date.basis: Date of the operation; reported in Nature 413:379–380 (2001).

milestones.whatChanged: A complete operation was shown to be possible with the surgeon on another continent.
milestones.whyItMattered: It demonstrated that a surgeon could operate across an ocean, a step towards bringing specialist surgery to places without specialist surgeons.
limitations: It was a single demonstration on one patient; it did not by itself make remote surgery routine.

sources.citation: Marescaux J, Leroy J, Gagner M, et al. Transatlantic robot-assisted telesurgery. Nature 413:379–380 (2001), as catalogued in Garrison–Morton (HistoryofMedicine.com).

milestones.title: Carlo Urbani raises the alarm over SARS in Hanoi
milestones.summary: In February–March 2003 Carlo Urbani, a WHO infectious disease specialist in Hanoi, recognised that a pneumonia spreading through the French Hospital was a new and dangerous disease. His warnings helped trigger isolation measures and a global alert. He died of SARS on 29 March 2003.
milestones.explanation:
A businessman with a high fever was admitted to the French Hospital in Hanoi on 26 February 2003. Urbani, asked to help on 28 February, saw hospital staff falling ill and concluded that this was a new and highly contagious disease. He alerted WHO headquarters and persuaded Vietnamese health officials to isolate patients, cordon off the hospital and screen travellers.

On 15 March WHO declared the disease Urbani had identified a worldwide health threat. Urbani developed symptoms on 11 March on a flight to Bangkok, and died there on 29 March after nearly three weeks in isolation. Viet Nam's quick containment of its outbreak is credited to resolute government action and to his early work.

date.basis: Urbani was called to the hospital on 28 February 2003, alerted WHO in early March and died on 29 March 2003.

people.name: Carlo Urbani
people.role: WHO communicable disease specialist in Viet Nam

milestones.whatChanged: Early isolation and infection control in Hanoi, and an early warning to WHO, helped turn a hospital cluster into an international alert.
milestones.whyItMattered: It is a prominent example of how one clinician's recognition of an unusual cluster can shape an epidemic response, and of the risks borne by health workers.
limitations: The outbreak had begun in Guangdong, China; Urbani traced the Hanoi patient's movements back there. His warning concerned its spread to Hanoi, not its origin.
Accounts differ by a few days on the exact dates of his warnings.

milestones.title: Face transplants: partial in Amiens, full in Barcelona
milestones.summary: In November 2005 surgeons in Amiens, France, transplanted the nose, lips and chin of a brain-dead donor onto Isabelle Dinoire, who had been disfigured in an animal attack. In March 2010 a team in Barcelona performed the first full face transplant.
milestones.explanation:
Transplanting a face, a composite of skin, muscle, nerves and sometimes bone, was debated for years because it requires lifelong immunosuppression for a procedure that is not life-saving. After the French national ethics committee accepted partial transplants while expressing reservations about full ones, Bernard Devauchelle and Jean-Michel Dubernard led the Amiens operation on 27 November 2005; Dubernard had performed the first hand transplant of the modern era in 1998.

Further partial transplants followed in China, France and the United States. In March 2010 a team led by Joan Pere Barret at Vall d'Hebron University Hospital in Barcelona replaced a man's whole face in one piece.

date.basis: Partial transplant on 27 November 2005; full face transplant in March 2010.

people.name: Joan Pere Barret
people.role: Plastic surgeon; led the Barcelona team

milestones.whatChanged: Severe facial disfigurement could be reconstructed with donor tissue that moves, feels and looks like a face, rather than only with grafts from the patient's own body.
milestones.whyItMattered: It extended transplantation to tissues that restore appearance, expression and function, with large effects on recipients' lives.
limitations: Recipients need lifelong immunosuppression, with risks of infection, cancer and rejection; some recipients have died of complications.
Only small numbers have been performed, so long-term outcomes rest on few cases.

milestones.title: Modified mRNA, from a 2005 finding to COVID-19 vaccines
milestones.summary: Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman found in 2005 that chemically modified building blocks stop synthetic mRNA from triggering inflammation. Their work enabled the mRNA vaccines against COVID-19 approved in December 2020.
milestones.explanation:
Using messenger RNA to make the body produce a vaccine antigen had been proposed decades earlier, but synthetic mRNA provoked inflammation and produced little protein. Working at the University of Pennsylvania, Karikó and Weissman showed that immune cells treat unmodified synthetic mRNA as foreign, and that changing its nucleoside bases almost abolished the reaction. They published in 2005; later studies showed that modified mRNA also produces much more protein.

When the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic began, this groundwork, combined with other advances and very large public and private investment, allowed two base-modified mRNA vaccines to be developed and tested at unprecedented speed. Both were approved in December 2020, with reported protection of around 95% against disease in their trials.

date.basis: Key publication in 2005; vaccine approvals in December 2020.

milestones.whatChanged: Made mRNA usable as a vaccine platform by removing its inflammatory effect and increasing protein production.
milestones.whyItMattered: Enabled highly effective COVID-19 vaccines within a year of the pandemic's start, and a platform now applied to other diseases.
limitations: The 2020 vaccines also depended on other advances, including lipid delivery and stabilised spike proteins.
Global access to COVID-19 vaccines was very unequal, especially in 2021.

sources.citation: The Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet. Press release: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 2023.
sources.supports: University of Pennsylvania; 2005 publication on base modifications abolishing inflammatory responses; 2008 and 2010 studies on protein production; two vaccines approved in December 2020 with ~95% reported protection.

sources.citation: The Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet. Scientific background 2023: discoveries concerning nucleoside base modifications that enabled the development of effective mRNA vaccines against COVID-19.
sources.supports: Concept proposed over 30 years earlier; stabilised spike antigen and large investments also required; approval of two vaccines in late 2020.

milestones.title: Rotavirus vaccines return after an early setback
milestones.summary: The original rotavirus vaccine, RotaShield, was withdrawn in 1999 after it was linked to a rare bowel blockage. Two new oral vaccines, RotaTeq and Rotarix, were each tested in 60,000–70,000 infants and introduced from 2006.
milestones.explanation:
Rotavirus causes severe diarrhoea in young children, some of whom become dangerously dehydrated. RotaShield, licensed in the United States in 1998, was withdrawn in 1999 when surveillance linked it to intussusception, a bowel blockage, in about 1 in 10,000 vaccinated infants.

The next vaccines were tested in exceptionally large trials designed to detect such a risk. RotaTeq, a bovine–human reassortant vaccine developed by H. Fred Clark, Stanley Plotkin and Paul Offit, was licensed in the United States in February 2006. Rotarix, an attenuated human strain from GSK, was reported effective in a large trial published the same year and licensed in the United States in 2008. Both are given as drops by mouth.

date.basis: RotaTeq licensed in the United States in February 2006; Rotarix trial results published in 2006. The withdrawn first vaccine dates from 1998–99.

milestones.locationNote: Both vaccines were tested in multinational trials and introduced in many countries; no single place is mapped.

people.name: H. Fred Clark, Stanley Plotkin and Paul Offit

milestones.whatChanged: Infants could be protected against severe rotavirus diarrhoea with oral vaccines whose safety had been tested in very large trials.
milestones.whyItMattered: Both vaccines are now recommended for use worldwide, protecting infants against a major cause of severe childhood diarrhoea.
limitations: A small increased risk of intussusception has been found after both newer vaccines, judged to be outweighed by their benefits.

sources.supports: RotaShield withdrawn in 1999 for risk of intussusception; RotaTeq licensed 2006; Rotarix licensed in the US 2008; each tested in about 60,000–70,000 infants before licensure.

milestones.title: An approved retinal implant restores some sight
milestones.summary: The Argus II retinal prosthesis, developed by Second Sight in California from work begun at Johns Hopkins, received European approval in 2011 and US approval in 2013. It gave some people blinded by retinitis pigmentosa limited, artificial vision.
milestones.explanation:
In retinitis pigmentosa the light-sensing cells of the retina die, but other retinal nerve cells survive. The Argus II stimulates those surviving cells with an array of 60 electrodes implanted on the retina.

The device received the CE mark in Europe in 2011 and US approval as a humanitarian use device in February 2013, after a trial in 30 patients. It was the first visual prosthesis to become commercially available; more than 350 people had been implanted by 2019.

date.basis: European CE mark in 2011; US FDA approval on 14 February 2013.

people.name: Mark Humayun and Robert Greenberg
people.role: Began developing a retinal prosthesis at Johns Hopkins University

milestones.whatChanged: Some people with profound blindness from retinal degeneration could perceive light, shapes and movement again.
milestones.whyItMattered: It showed that an electronic implant could provide useful, if limited, vision, and established a path for later visual prostheses.
limitations: The vision provided is crude and far from normal sight.
US approval was as a humanitarian use device, which did not require proof of effectiveness.
In 2019 the company announced that it would concentrate on a brain implant instead.

milestones.title: Uterus transplants lead to births
milestones.summary: In 2011 surgeons in Antalya, Turkey, transplanted a uterus from a deceased donor, and the recipient later became pregnant. In 2014 a woman in Gothenburg, Sweden, gave birth after receiving a uterus from a living donor, the first live birth after uterus transplantation.
milestones.explanation:
Women born without a uterus or who have lost it could not carry a pregnancy. After a failed attempt in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, in 2000 and years of animal research, a team at Akdeniz University Hospital in Antalya led by Ömer Özkan carried out a transplant from a deceased donor in 2011, and the recipient later became pregnant.

In Sweden, Mats Brännström's team at Sahlgrenska University Hospital began a trial of transplants from living donors in 2012. In 2014 one recipient, a 35-year-old woman born without a uterus, gave birth to a healthy boy, reported in The Lancet as proof of concept.

date.basis: Turkish deceased-donor transplant in 2011; Swedish birth in 2014 (published online 6 October 2014).

people.name: Ömer Özkan
people.role: Plastic surgeon; led the Antalya team

milestones.whatChanged: Women with absolute uterine-factor infertility could carry their own pregnancy.
milestones.whyItMattered: It created a new option for a form of infertility previously treatable only by adoption or surrogacy.
limitations: The procedures involve major surgery for donor and recipient and temporary immunosuppression.
Numbers remain small; the first birth from a deceased-donor uterus was reported in Brazil only in 2017.

milestones.title: A 3D-printed implant replaces the top of a skull
milestones.summary: Surgeons at University Medical Center Utrecht replaced most of the skull of a 22-year-old woman, whose bone had thickened to compress her brain, with a custom 3D-printed plastic implant. The 23-hour operation was announced in March 2014.
milestones.explanation:
The patient had a rare condition in which her skull kept thickening, to about 5 cm, causing headaches, loss of vision and poor coordination. Skull defects had previously been repaired with cement shaped by hand during surgery. Led by the neurosurgeon Bon Verweij, the Utrecht team removed the top of her skull and fitted a plastic implant printed to the exact shape of her head by the Australian company Anatomics.

The hospital waited three months before announcing the operation in March 2014, by which time the patient was symptom-free and back at work.

people.name: Anatomics
people.role: Australian company that printed the implant

milestones.whatChanged: A large section of skull could be replaced with an implant printed to fit an individual patient exactly.
milestones.whyItMattered: It illustrated how 3D printing can produce patient-specific implants, now widely used in skull and facial reconstruction.
limitations: Smaller 3D-printed skull implants had been used before, including by the same surgeon; the novelty was replacing most of the cranium.
The sources available are press reports of the hospital's announcement; we did not find a peer-reviewed case report.

milestones.title: Growing organs in the laboratory: kidney, liver and heart
milestones.summary: In 2013 teams in Boston and Yokohama grew a working rat kidney on a stripped-down organ scaffold and a vascularised human liver bud from stem cells. In 2019 a team in Tel Aviv 3D-printed a small heart from a patient's own cells. None has yet been used in patients.
milestones.explanation:
The shortage of donor organs has driven efforts to build organs in the laboratory. At Massachusetts General Hospital, Harald Ott's team washed the cells out of rat kidneys, leaving a collagen scaffold, repopulated it with new cells and transplanted the result into rats, where it produced urine. At Yokohama City University, Takanori Takebe and Hideki Taniguchi's team grew 'liver buds' from human induced pluripotent stem cells that connected to the blood supply when transplanted into mice and rescued them from liver failure.

In 2019 Tal Dvir's group at Tel Aviv University printed a heart the size of a rabbit's, with blood vessels and chambers, from fatty tissue taken from patients.

date.basis: Kidney and liver studies published in April and July 2013; printed heart announced in April 2019.

milestones.whatChanged: Laboratory-built organ tissue was shown to connect to a living blood supply and perform some organ functions in animals.
milestones.whyItMattered: These proofs of concept point towards organs made to order from a patient's own cells, which would avoid both donor shortages and rejection.
limitations: All three were laboratory or animal studies; none produced an organ used in a person.
Producing such tissue in the quantities needed for human transplantation was not yet possible.

milestones.title: Ring vaccination trial against Ebola in Guinea
milestones.summary: During the 2013–16 West African Ebola epidemic, the Ebola ça Suffit! trial in Guinea vaccinated contacts, and contacts of contacts, of confirmed cases either immediately or after 21 days. No one vaccinated immediately developed Ebola from ten days onwards.
milestones.explanation:
Testing a vaccine during a fast-moving epidemic is difficult. The trial, run by Guinean authorities with WHO, Médecins Sans Frontières and other partners, used ring vaccination, the containment strategy that had helped eradicate smallpox. Each newly confirmed case defined a ring of contacts and contacts of contacts, and rings were randomly assigned to immediate or delayed vaccination with a single dose of rVSV-ZEBOV.

Among those vaccinated immediately there were no cases of Ebola with onset ten or more days after randomisation, while cases did occur in the delayed group. The final results, published in 2017, estimated vaccine efficacy at 100 per cent, with wide statistical uncertainty.

The vaccine was later used in further outbreaks and real-world studies found it highly effective. The trial showed that rigorous evaluation can be done in the middle of an emergency in a low-income country.

date.basis: Trial conducted in 2015; interim results published in 2015 and final results in The Lancet in February 2017.

milestones.whyItMattered: Supported the vaccine's use in later Ebola outbreaks and demonstrated a rigorous trial design suited to emergencies.
limitations: The efficacy estimate had wide confidence intervals because the epidemic was waning.
Some researchers questioned aspects of the analysis; later real-world studies supported high effectiveness.
milestones.contested: A published letter questioned how efficacy was calculated; subsequent outbreak studies nonetheless found the vaccine highly effective.

milestones.title: An 'artificial pancreas' adjusts insulin automatically
milestones.summary: In September 2016 the US FDA approved Medtronic's MiniMed 670G, the first hybrid closed-loop system for type 1 diabetes. A sensor measures glucose every five minutes and a pump adjusts background insulin automatically.
milestones.explanation:
People with type 1 diabetes must constantly check their glucose and dose insulin, usually with injections or a pump that they program themselves. A system in which a glucose sensor automatically controls an insulin pump, a 'closed loop', is often called an artificial pancreas.

The MiniMed 670G was approved on 28 September 2016 for people aged 14 and over, after a study of 123 participants. It measures glucose every five minutes and automatically sets background (basal) insulin; users still give mealtime doses themselves, which is why it is called a hybrid system and was seen as a step towards a fully closed loop.

date.basis: Date of FDA approval.

milestones.locationNote: A regulatory approval of a device tested at several centres; no single place is mapped.
milestones.whatChanged: Part of the work of managing type 1 diabetes, adjusting background insulin day and night, could be handed to an automated system.
milestones.whyItMattered: It was the first approved system to hand part of insulin dosing to an automated controller.
limitations: Users still had to count carbohydrates and give mealtime doses.
Approval was based on a three-month study of 123 people.
'First' refers to approval by the US regulator, not to the first closed-loop system ever built or tested.

milestones.title: First malaria vaccine recommended for children
milestones.summary: On 6 October 2021 WHO recommended broad use of the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine for children in areas with moderate to high transmission, based on a pilot programme in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi.
milestones.explanation:
From 2019, the health ministries of Ghana, Kenya and Malawi introduced the RTS,S vaccine into routine childhood immunisation in selected areas, as a pilot coordinated by WHO. By the time of the recommendation, the programme had reached more than 800,000 children.

After reviewing two years of data on safety, feasibility and impact, WHO's advisory bodies recommended the vaccine for children in sub-Saharan Africa and other regions with moderate to high transmission of Plasmodium falciparum. It was the first vaccine recommended against any human parasitic disease. A second vaccine, R21/Matrix-M, was recommended in October 2023.

WHO presents the vaccine as an addition to existing tools such as bed nets and prompt treatment, not a replacement for them.

date.basis: Pilot introduction from 2019; WHO recommendation on 6 October 2021.

people.name: Ministries of Health of Ghana, Kenya and Malawi

milestones.whyItMattered: Malaria remains a leading cause of death among young children in Africa; the vaccine reduces severe disease.

The vaccine is meant to be used on top of existing malaria control measures, not instead of them.
The recommendation followed a pilot in three countries; impact elsewhere depends on how the vaccine is delivered.

milestones.title: The last 8% of a human genome is sequenced
milestones.summary: In 2022 the Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) Consortium published a complete, gapless 3.055-billion-base-pair sequence of a human genome. It covered every chromosome except Y, including the repetitive regions the Human Genome Project could not finish.
milestones.explanation:
The reference human genome released from 2000 onwards covered the gene-rich parts of the chromosomes but left about 8% unfinished: highly repetitive regions such as centromeres and the arrays of ribosomal DNA genes, which the short sequence reads of the time could not piece together. That missing 8% is comparable in size to a whole chromosome.

The T2T Consortium, led by researchers at the US National Human Genome Research Institute, the University of California, Santa Cruz, and the University of Washington, used newer long-read sequencing on a cell line that carries only one copy of each chromosome, which made the repeats easier to assemble. Their main paper, one of six in Science on 1 April 2022, reported gapless sequences for all chromosomes except Y, corrected errors in the earlier reference and added nearly 200 million base pairs of new sequence.

date.basis: Published online in Science on 31 March 2022 (print issue of 1 April 2022).

locations.name: National Human Genome Research Institute, Bethesda

milestones.locationNote: The consortium involved many institutions; the map shows the three that led it.

people.name: Adam Phillippy, Karen Miga and Evan Eichler
people.role: Consortium leaders (NHGRI, UC Santa Cruz and University of Washington)

milestones.whatChanged: Researchers could study the repetitive parts of the genome, such as centromeres, that had been missing from the reference for two decades, and found more than 2 million additional variants using the new sequence.
milestones.whyItMattered: A gap-free reference makes it possible to look for disease-related variation in regions that were previously invisible, and to compare genomes more accurately.
limitations: Chromosome Y was not included in the 2022 paper.
It is the sequence of a single cell line, so on its own it cannot represent variation between people.
"Complete" refers to this one genome; it does not mean that the function of all its sequence is understood.

sources.supports: Complete 3.055-billion-base-pair sequence (T2T-CHM13); gapless assemblies for all chromosomes except Y; remaining 8% of the genome; reference since 2000 covered only the euchromatic fraction; errors corrected; nearly 200 million base pairs of new sequence; ribosomal DNA arrays; NHGRI affiliation of lead authors.

sources.supports: Publication date; leadership from NHGRI, UC Santa Cruz and the University of Washington; NHGRI as primary funder; cell line with one copy of each chromosome; longer sequence reads; more than 2 million additional variants; six papers in Science; the last 8% comparable in size to a chromosome.

stories.title: Taming pain: the development of anaesthesia
stories.dek: From Ice Age surgery with no record of pain relief to herbal and then chemical anaesthesia, reached independently in Japan and the United States.

steps.note: Surgery long predates any record of anaesthesia. How this Ice Age patient's pain and bleeding were managed is simply unknown.
Andean surgeons operated on the skull for nearly two thousand years, with survival improving over time. No written record tells us what, if anything, eased the pain.
In 1804 Hanaoka Seishū used a herbal preparation to anaesthetise a patient fully for breast surgery, the earliest well-documented general anaesthetic.
Four decades later, and with no knowledge of Hanaoka's work, ether was used in Georgia and then demonstrated publicly in Boston. Publicity, not priority, drove its spread.
An 1879 account from Bunyoro describes banana wine used to dull pain during a caesarean section, a reminder that pain control took many forms.
Reliable anaesthesia, together with antisepsis and blood transfusion, made long, complex operations such as heart transplantation possible.

stories.title: Understanding and preventing infection
stories.dek: People learned to block the spread of disease long before they knew what caused it, and identifying germs did not immediately bring cures.

steps.note: Ragusa's 1377 rule separated travellers for 30 days. It worked on observation, centuries before anyone knew about plague bacteria.
Semmelweis's chlorinated-lime handwashing cut maternal deaths in Vienna in 1847, but his colleagues resisted and the practice lapsed.
John Snow linked cholera to a water pump in 1854 while most doctors still blamed foul air. The famous map came after the investigation, not before.
Drawing on Pasteur's work, Lister used carbolic acid to prevent wound infection, turning germ theory into surgical practice.
Laveran found the malaria parasite in Algeria in 1880, the first protozoan shown to cause disease, and was doubted for nearly a decade.
Koch identified the tuberculosis bacillus in 1882, but effective drugs took another sixty years.
Knowing how a disease travels can matter as much as knowing its cause: mosquitoes became the target of malaria control.
Fleming's 1928 observation sat largely unused for a decade until others turned it into a medicine.
A cheap drink of sugar and salt, proven in Dhaka and the 1971 refugee camps, became one of the most effective responses to deadly diarrhoea.

stories.title: Vaccination and disease eradication
stories.dek: Inoculation travelled from Asia and Africa to Europe and the Americas, became vaccination, and eventually ended smallpox.

steps.note: Deliberately giving a mild smallpox infection was practised in China, Africa and the Ottoman world long before Europe adopted it.
In Boston, knowledge from an enslaved African man, Onesimus, led to inoculation and to an early attempt to judge it by counting deaths.
Jenner tested and publicised cowpox, a safer substitute. A Dorset farmer had already tried it on his family.
Vaccine crossed oceans in the bodies of orphaned children, an achievement inseparable from its ethical cost.
Twentieth-century vaccines were tested in trials of unprecedented size, in the United States and, during the Cold War, in the Soviet Union.
Case-finding and containment, not just mass vaccination, ended smallpox. The last natural case was in Somalia in 1977.
The same ring strategy was used to test an Ebola vaccine in Guinea during an epidemic.
The first vaccine against a human parasite was recommended in 2021 after pilots led by health ministries in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi.
Fifteen years of largely unheralded laboratory work made mRNA vaccines possible within a year of the COVID-19 pandemic's start.

stories.title: Seeing inside the body
stories.dek: From reading signs on the surface to listening, cutting and finally imaging, with long gaps where knowledge was lost or ignored.

steps.note: An Egyptian surgeon described the surface of the brain in skull wounds, recording what injuries revealed.
Babylonian scholars organised diagnosis as a reference work linking outward signs to what was happening within.
Ibn al-Nafis reasoned that blood passes through the lungs, a correct insight forgotten in the West for nearly seven centuries.
Vesalius made dissection and accurate illustration the basis of anatomy, using the bodies of executed criminals.
The stethoscope let doctors hear disease in the chest and check their judgements against autopsy.
X-rays showed the inside of the living body without surgery and were adopted with extraordinary speed.
Computing turned X-rays into slices through the body, revealing soft tissue such as the brain.

stories.title: Making childbirth safer
stories.dek: Knowledge about pregnancy and birth has been written down for nearly 4,000 years; the obstacles have often been secrecy, resistance and access.

steps.note: Egypt's oldest surviving medical papyrus is devoted to women's health, fertility and pregnancy.
A family of London practitioners kept a life-saving instrument secret for over a century.
Handwashing slashed deaths from childbed fever in Vienna, yet the evidence was resisted.
In 1879 a European visitor watched a caesarean in Bunyoro in which mother and child survived, at a time when the operation was often fatal in European hospitals.
A sheep experiment in Auckland led to a randomised trial showing that steroids before birth protect premature babies.
Short of incubators, doctors in Bogotá turned parents' bodies into the incubator. Trials later confirmed the benefit.

stories.title: Caring for the mind
stories.dek: Explanations of mental illness and ways of caring for it, from Greek arguments against divine causes to community care in Belgium and Nigeria.

steps.note: A Greek author insisted that epilepsy had natural causes in the brain, though stigma long outlasted the argument.
Pilgrims seeking cures at Geel were boarded with local families, the start of a tradition of community care that continues today.
Cairo's great hospital included wards for mental illness within a general, endowed institution.
A small uncontrolled study in Melbourne revived lithium, later confirmed by a placebo-controlled trial in Denmark.
At Aro in Nigeria, patients lived in villages during treatment, an influential model of culturally grounded community psychiatry.
